paper_context.research_question: How do readability and question difficulty (prerequisite skills) relate in reading comprehension datasets, and what are the qualitative characteristics of existing RC datasets according to these two dimensions?
contribution_style: grounded in psychological theory (Construction-Integration model, McNamara & Magliano)
cross-disciplinary synthesis (NLP entailment, psychology, readability research)
systematic annotation study with inter-annotator agreement reporting
comparative analysis across six existing datasets
main_claims: Readability of RC dataset texts does not directly correlate with question difficulty (weak correlations 0.025–0.416)
It is possible to construct RC datasets that are easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer (exemplified by MCTest)
A refined taxonomy of 13 prerequisite skills (reorganized from prior work) provides more theoretically grounded classification than previous studies
Two classes of metrics—prerequisite skills and readability—together characterize RC dataset quality more comprehensively than existing superficial categorizations
Different RC datasets exhibit distinct profiles: QA4MRE is difficult on both dimensions; SQuAD is difficult-to-read but easy-to-answer; MCTest is easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer
expected_evaluation_dimensions: Validity and theoretical grounding of the 13-skill taxonomy (alignment with psychology literature, entailment theory, and prior RC work)
Reliability of annotation procedure (inter-annotator agreement, consistency across datasets)
Empirical findings: strength and interpretation of correlations between prerequisite skills and readability metrics
Utility of the framework for dataset construction and system development (curriculum learning applicability)
Scope and limitations: coverage of six datasets, sample size (100 questions per dataset), exclusion rationale for other datasets
Methodological limitations acknowledged: inability to evaluate sentence selection competence, treatment of 'no answer' questions, definition of 'solvable' questions
Generalizability: applicability to future RC datasets and systems beyond the analyzed benchmarks

extracted_claims.claim_label: Weak correlation between readability and question difficulty
extracted_claims.claim_text: Readability of RC dataset texts does not directly correlate with question difficulty; correlations range from 0.025–0.416 across datasets
evidence: Table 5 presents Pearson's correlation coefficients between the number of required prerequisite skills and each readability metric for all questions of the RC datasets. Although there are weak correlations from 0.025 to 0.416, the results highlight that there is not necessarily a strong correlation between the two values.
Figure 3 shows trends of datasets: QA4MRE was relatively difficult both to read and to answer, and SQuAD was difficult to read but easy to answer.
This leads to the following two insights. First, the readability of RC datasets does not directly affect the difficulty of their questions.
uncertainty_flags: Correlation strength interpretation depends on domain conventions; 0.025–0.416 range spans weak to moderate, but no threshold for 'direct correlation' is formally defined
Sample size per dataset is 100 questions; generalizability to larger samples or other datasets not empirically tested
Readability metrics applied only to sentences selected by annotators as necessary; does not reflect full document readability
Pearson correlation assumes linear relationship; non-linear associations not explored

extracted_claims.claim_label: Easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer datasets are constructible
extracted_claims.claim_text: It is possible to construct RC datasets that are easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer, exemplified by MCTest
extracted_claims.section_anchor: Section 1, Introduction; Section 5, Results; Section 6, Discussion
evidence: In the second example from MCTest (Richardson et al., 2013), the document is written for children and is easy to read, but the question requires reading multiple sentences and a combination of several skills, such as understanding of causal relations, coreference resolution, and complementing ellipsis.
MCTest is a good example of an RC dataset that is easy to read but difficult to answer. The corpus' genre (i.e., narrative) seems to reflect the trend of required skills for the questions.
Table 4 shows MCTest had the lowest readability scores; Table 3 shows MCTest questions required average 1.56 skills (moderate difficulty).
uncertainty_flags: MCTest is a single exemplar; no systematic construction methodology provided for replicating this property
Difficulty assessment relies on annotator judgment of prerequisite skills; no independent validation against system performance
Genre (narrative vs. expository) is confounded with readability; causal mechanism not isolated
Sample size (100 questions) may not be representative of full MCTest dataset characteristics

extracted_claims.claim_label: Refined 13-skill taxonomy provides theoretically grounded classification
extracted_claims.claim_text: A reorganized taxonomy of 13 prerequisite skills (from prior 10-skill work) provides more theoretically grounded classification than previous studies, grounded in psychology (C–I model, bridging/elaboration) and entailment theory
evidence: We reorganized the category of knowledge reasoning in terms of textual entailment and human text comprehension. In research on textual entailment, several methodologies have been proposed for precise analysis of entailment phenomena (Dagan et al., 2013; LoBue and Yates, 2011). In psychology research, Kintsch (1993) proposed dichotomies for the classification of human inferences: retrieved versus generated. In addition, McNamara and Magliano (2009) proposed a similar distinction for inferences: bridging versus elaboration.
Skills 8–10 (Ellipsis, Bridging, Elaboration) are explicitly grounded in psychology and entailment literature.

A problem in previous studies, including that of Sugawara and Aizawa (2016), is that they analyzed only two datasets and that their categorization of knowledge reasoning is provisional with a weak theoretical background.
uncertainty_flags: Theoretical grounding is asserted but not formally validated; no empirical test of whether the 13-skill taxonomy better predicts system performance than prior 10-skill taxonomy
Mapping between psychology concepts (bridging/elaboration) and NLP entailment phenomena is conceptual; no formal alignment procedure described
Inter-annotator agreement (90.1% on 62 questions) is reported but not broken down by skill; some skills may have lower reliability
No comparison of annotation consistency between old and new taxonomies

extracted_claims.claim_label: Two-class metric framework characterizes RC datasets more comprehensively
extracted_claims.claim_text: Two classes of metrics—prerequisite skills and readability—together characterize RC dataset quality more comprehensively than existing superficial categorizations (e.g., question type, answer type)
evidence: In these situations, it is difficult to assess systems accurately. As Norvig (1989) stated, questions easy for humans often turn out to be difficult for systems.

However, a current problem is that most RC datasets are presented only with superficial categories, such as question types (e.g., what, where, and who) and answer types (e.g., numeric, location, and person).
We adopt two classes of evaluation metrics to show the qualitative features of RC datasets.
uncertainty_flags: Comprehensiveness is asserted but not quantitatively measured; no metric for comparing framework expressiveness
No empirical demonstration that systems trained with knowledge of these two classes perform better than systems trained without
Readability metrics are borrowed from second-language acquisition literature; applicability to RC system development not validated
Framework does not address other potentially relevant dimensions (e.g., answer type, question type, context length)

extracted_claims.claim_label: Dataset-specific profiles characterize six RC datasets
extracted_claims.claim_text: Different RC datasets exhibit distinct profiles: QA4MRE is difficult on both dimensions; SQuAD is difficult-to-read but easy-to-answer; MCTest is easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer; MS MARCO is easiest; Who-did-What and NewsQA occupy intermediate positions
evidence: QA4MRE seemed to be the most difficult dataset among the RC datasets we analyzed, whereas MS MARCO seemed to be the easiest.
SQuAD was difficult to read along with QA4MRE but relatively easy to answer compared to other datasets.
MCTest is a good example of an RC dataset that is easy to read but difficult to answer.
Table 3: QA4MRE average 3.25 skills; MCTest 1.56; SQuAD 1.28; MS MARCO 1.19.
Table 4: SQuAD and QA4MRE achieved the highest scores in most metrics; MCTest had the lowest scores.
uncertainty_flags: Profiles are based on 100 questions per dataset; may not represent full dataset distributions
Difficulty rankings are relative to this sample; absolute difficulty thresholds not defined
Confounding factors: dataset size, curation method, genre, and task formulation all vary; isolating contribution of each unclear
No statistical significance testing of differences between datasets

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The number of required prerequisite skills directly corresponds to question difficulty
supporting_evidence: That study presented an important observation of the relation between the difficulty of an RC task and prerequisite skills: the more skills that are required to answer a question, the more difficult the question is. From this observation, we assume that the number of required skills corresponds to the difficulty of a question.
This is because each skill corresponds to a function of a system, which has to be equipped with the system.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If skill count does not linearly map to difficulty, the entire framework for characterizing dataset difficulty becomes invalid. System development using curriculum learning (easy-to-difficult progression) may not follow the intended learning trajectory.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Readability metrics computed on selected sentences reflect the readability difficulty experienced by systems answering questions
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 3.2, Readability Metrics; Section 4.1, Annotation Procedure
supporting_evidence: We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions.

Nonetheless, because these metrics were proposed for human readability, they do not necessarily correlate with those for RC systems. Therefore, in a system analysis, we ideally have to consult various features.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: Readability scores may not reflect actual difficulty for RC systems. The weak correlations observed may be artifacts of using human-oriented readability metrics rather than evidence of true independence between readability and question difficulty.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Annotators can reliably identify which sentences are necessary to answer a question
supporting_evidence: The annotators then selected sentences that needed to be read to answer the question and decided if each prerequisite skill was required.
As mentioned in Section 1, our methodology cannot evaluate the competence of selecting sentences that need to be read to answer questions.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If annotators systematically over- or under-select sentences, readability metrics will be biased. Skill annotations may be inconsistent if sentence selection is unreliable. The authors acknowledge this limitation but do not quantify its impact.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The 13 prerequisite skills are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive for RC tasks
supporting_evidence: By refining Sugawara et al. (2017)'s ten reading comprehension skills, we reorganized thirteen prerequisite skills in total.
We allowed multiple labeling [of skills per question].
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If skills overlap or if important skills are missing, the taxonomy will not provide a complete characterization. Multiple labeling is allowed, suggesting non-exclusivity, but the framework does not address potential redundancy or gaps.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Inter-annotator agreement of 90.1% on 62 questions generalizes to the full annotation set (600 questions across 6 datasets)
supporting_evidence: The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If agreement varies significantly across datasets or skill types, the reliability of dataset characterizations is compromised. The sample of 62 questions (10% of total) may not be representative of all 600 annotated questions.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Pearson correlation coefficient is the appropriate measure of association between prerequisite skills and readability metrics
supporting_evidence: Table 5 presents Pearson's correlation coefficients between the number of required prerequisite skills and each readability metric for all questions of the RC datasets.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the relationship is non-linear, monotonic but non-linear, or mediated by dataset-specific factors, Pearson correlation will underestimate or mischaracterize the association. Spearman rank correlation or other methods might reveal different patterns.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: A random sample of 100 questions per dataset is sufficient to characterize the dataset's overall properties
supporting_evidence: For the annotation, we randomly selected 100 questions from each dataset in Table 1. This amount of questions was considered to be sufficient for the analysis of RC datasets as performed by Chen et al. (2016).
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If datasets have heterogeneous subsets (e.g., by topic, difficulty, or source), a sample of 100 may not capture the full distribution. Confidence intervals or bootstrap resampling would strengthen claims about dataset-level properties.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: The Construction-Integration (C–I) model and McNamara & Magliano's framework are appropriate theoretical foundations for RC dataset evaluation
identified_assumptions.section_anchor: Section 2.2, Reading Comprehension in Psychology; Section 3, Evaluation Metrics
supporting_evidence: Our two classes of metrics are based on McNamara and Magliano (2009)'s analysis of human text comprehension in psychology.
Based on McNamara and Magliano (2009)'s depiction of text comprehension, we adopted two classes for the evaluation of RC datasets: prerequisite skills and readability.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If the C–I model does not accurately describe how RC systems process text, the framework may not be predictive of system performance. The framework is grounded in human cognition, not machine learning; applicability to neural systems is unvalidated.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Readability metrics from Vajjala & Meurers (2012) are appropriate for characterizing RC dataset difficulty
supporting_evidence: Of these, we used the classification of linguistic features proposed by Vajjala and Meurers (2012). This is because they presented a comparison of a wide range of linguistic features focusing on second language acquisition and their method can be applied to plain text.
Nonetheless, because these metrics were proposed for human readability, they do not necessarily correlate with those for RC systems.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: The authors acknowledge that human readability metrics may not correlate with RC system difficulty. The weak correlations observed may reflect this mismatch rather than true independence of readability and question difficulty.

identified_assumptions.assumption_text: Questions labeled as 'nonsense' or 'unsolvable' can be reliably identified and excluded from analysis
supporting_evidence: The annotators were allowed to select nonsense for an unsolvable question to distinguish it from a solvable question that required no skills.
There were questions for which there were disagreements regarding the decision of nonsense. For example, some questions can be solved by external knowledge without seeing their context.
identified_assumptions.risk_if_unmet: If 'nonsense' is ambiguous or context-dependent, the filtering of questions will be inconsistent. This affects the characterization of datasets like MS MARCO and Who-did-What, which had higher nonsense rates.

argument_focus: Empirical characterization of six RC datasets along two dimensions: prerequisite skills and readability
Demonstration that readability and question difficulty are weakly correlated (0.025–0.416)
Refinement and theoretical grounding of a 13-skill taxonomy for RC
Proposal that two-class metric framework (skills + readability) provides more comprehensive dataset evaluation than superficial categories
Exemplification of dataset design space: easy-to-read/difficult-to-answer (MCTest), difficult-to-read/easy-to-answer (SQuAD), difficult-on-both (QA4MRE)
contribution_targets: Dataset annotation and analysis: systematic annotation of 600 questions across 6 datasets with inter-annotator agreement reporting
Metric refinement: reorganization of prerequisite skills from 10 to 13 categories with explicit grounding in psychology and entailment theory
Methodological framework: two-class evaluation framework (prerequisite skills + readability) for characterizing RC dataset quality
Empirical characterization: dataset profiles showing distinct difficulty patterns across readability and skill dimensions
Practical guidance: curriculum learning application—datasets can be ordered by difficulty for stepwise system development
evaluation_targets: Validity of the 13-skill taxonomy: Does it align with psychology literature (C–I model, bridging/elaboration) and entailment theory? Is it more theoretically grounded than prior 10-skill taxonomy?
Reliability of annotation: Is 90.1% inter-annotator agreement on 62 questions representative of full 600-question set? Does agreement vary by skill or dataset?
Empirical findings: Are correlations (0.025–0.416) statistically significant? Do they hold across different correlation measures (Spearman, Kendall)? Are differences between datasets significant?
Generalizability: Do findings hold for datasets not included (CNN/Daily Mail, CBTest, LAMBADA)? Are results sensitive to sample size (100 questions per dataset)?

Utility for system development: Does curriculum learning based on this framework improve RC system performance? Can the framework predict which datasets are suitable for training specific system architectures?

Methodological limitations: How much does the inability to evaluate sentence selection competence affect skill annotations? How are 'no answer' questions handled? What is the impact of readability metrics being human-oriented rather than system-oriented?
Scope and coverage: Why were certain datasets excluded (CNN/Daily Mail, CBTest, LAMBADA)? Are exclusion criteria justified? Do they bias the sample toward higher-quality datasets?
uncertainty_flags: Correlation strength interpretation: 0.025–0.416 range spans weak to moderate; no formal threshold for 'direct correlation' defined; interpretation depends on domain conventions
Sample representativeness: 100 questions per dataset is 10% of typical dataset size; confidence intervals or bootstrap analysis would strengthen claims
Confounding factors: Dataset differences in curation method, genre, task formulation, and size are not isolated; causal mechanisms unclear
Readability metric applicability: Metrics designed for human readability; applicability to RC systems not validated; weak correlations may reflect metric mismatch rather than true independence
Skill taxonomy validation: Theoretical grounding asserted but not empirically tested; no comparison of predictive power vs. prior 10-skill taxonomy; inter-annotator agreement not broken down by skill
Sentence selection reliability: Authors acknowledge inability to evaluate sentence selection competence; impact on skill annotations not quantified
Generalizability: Findings based on 6 datasets; applicability to future datasets or systems beyond analyzed benchmarks not tested
Statistical significance: No significance testing reported for differences between datasets or correlations
Non-linear relationships: Pearson correlation assumes linearity; non-linear or dataset-specific associations not explored
External knowledge in questions: Authors note ambiguity in identifying questions solvable by external knowledge; impact on 'nonsense' classification unclear
chaining_notes: For downstream reviewers: C1 (weak correlation claim) is central to the paper's main contribution. Verify that correlation coefficients are correctly computed and that the range 0.025–0.416 is not an artifact of sample size or metric choice. Consider whether Spearman or other measures would yield different conclusions.

For downstream reviewers: C3 (13-skill taxonomy) requires validation against prior work. Request comparison of annotation consistency between old and new taxonomies, and evidence that the new taxonomy better predicts system performance or human difficulty judgments.

For downstream reviewers: A2 (readability metrics reflect system difficulty) is a critical assumption. The authors acknowledge it may not hold; request empirical validation by correlating readability metrics with actual RC system performance on these datasets.

For downstream reviewers: A3 (sentence selection reliability) is acknowledged as a limitation but not quantified. Request inter-annotator agreement specifically for sentence selection, and sensitivity analysis showing how variation in sentence selection affects skill annotations.

For downstream reviewers: The claim that MCTest is 'easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer' (C2) relies on genre (narrative) as explanation. Request analysis isolating genre effects from other confounds (e.g., question generation method, answer type distribution).
For downstream reviewers: Curriculum learning application (Section 6) is speculative. Request empirical validation: train RC systems on datasets ordered by difficulty and measure learning curves.
For downstream reviewers: Dataset exclusion rationale (Section 4.2) may introduce bias. Verify that excluded datasets (CNN/Daily Mail, CBTest, LAMBADA) would not change the main findings if included.
For downstream reviewers: Inter-annotator agreement (90.1% on 62 questions) is reported globally. Request breakdown by skill and dataset to identify potential weak points in the taxonomy.
For downstream reviewers: The paper does not report statistical significance of correlations or differences between datasets. Request p-values, confidence intervals, and effect sizes.

For downstream reviewers: Readability metrics are applied only to selected sentences, not full documents. Request analysis of how this affects metric distributions and correlations compared to full-document readability.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper presents a systematic empirical study of six reading comprehension (RC) datasets using two evaluation dimensions: prerequisite skills (13-skill taxonomy) and readability metrics (10 linguistic features). The core logical argument is: (1) RC datasets vary along two independent dimensions (readability and question difficulty); (2) a refined 13-skill taxonomy provides theoretically grounded characterization; (3) weak correlations (0.025–0.416) between readability and skill count demonstrate that easy-to-read datasets can have difficult questions. The paper's reasoning chain is generally coherent and well-structured, moving from motivation → theoretical grounding → methodology → empirical results → dataset profiles. However, critical assumptions underlying the main claims are either asserted without empirical validation (e.g., skill count = difficulty) or acknowledged as limitations (e.g., readability metrics may not reflect system difficulty). The paper's strength lies in systematic annotation and cross-dataset comparison; its weakness lies in the gap between psychological theory (human comprehension) and practical applicability (RC system development). The logical argument does not break, but several inference steps require stronger evidentiary support.
logical_argument_graph: Motivation: RC systems need evaluation beyond superficial categories (question type, answer type) → Problem statement established via Figure 1 examples
Theoretical foundation: McNamara & Magliano (2009) C–I model proposes two aspects of comprehension (strategic/skilled + text ease) → Maps to two metric classes (prerequisite skills + readability)

Skill taxonomy refinement: Prior 10-skill taxonomy (Sugawara et al. 2017) lacks theoretical grounding → Reorganize into 13 skills using psychology (bridging/elaboration) and entailment theory (Dagan et al.) → Claim C3: new taxonomy is more theoretically grounded

Readability metrics: Adopt Vajjala & Meurers (2012) 10 linguistic features → Apply only to annotator-selected sentences → Acknowledge limitation: metrics designed for human readability, not RC systems (A2 risk)
Annotation procedure: Three annotators label 600 questions (100 per dataset) with skills and select necessary sentences → Inter-annotator agreement 90.1% on 62 questions (A5 generalization risk)

Empirical finding: Compute Pearson correlations between skill count and readability metrics → Result: weak correlations (0.025–0.416) across datasets → Claim C1: readability does not directly correlate with question difficulty

Dataset characterization: Plot datasets on 2D space (readability vs. skill count) → Identify three profiles: QA4MRE (difficult-both), SQuAD (difficult-read/easy-answer), MCTest (easy-read/difficult-answer) → Claim C5: datasets exhibit distinct profiles
Practical implication: Curriculum learning application—order datasets by difficulty for stepwise system development → Speculative claim not empirically validated

Logical coherence assessment: The chain from theory → metrics → annotation → correlation → dataset profiles is sound. However, the inference from weak correlation to 'readability does not affect difficulty' assumes linearity (A6) and ignores confounds (dataset curation, genre, task formulation). The claim that skill count = difficulty (A1) is asserted but not validated against system performance or human judgments.

strengths.title: Systematic cross-dataset annotation with inter-annotator agreement reporting
strengths.description: The paper annotates 600 questions across 6 datasets with consistent methodology and reports 90.1% inter-annotator agreement on a sample of 62 questions. This provides a solid empirical foundation for dataset characterization and enables comparative analysis.
evidence: Section 4.1: 'We asked three annotators to annotate questions of RC datasets with the prerequisite skills that are required to answer each question.'
Section 5: 'The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions.'
Appendix A: Detailed sampling methodology for each dataset ensures representativeness within each dataset's structure.

strengths.title: Theoretically grounded skill taxonomy with explicit psychology and NLP foundations
strengths.description: The 13-skill taxonomy is explicitly grounded in McNamara & Magliano's C–I model, Kintsch's inference dichotomies, and textual entailment theory. This provides stronger theoretical justification than the prior 10-skill taxonomy, which the authors note lacked theoretical background.
evidence: Section 3.1: Skills 8–10 (Ellipsis, Bridging, Elaboration) are explicitly mapped to psychology (bridging/elaboration) and entailment theory (Dagan et al., LoBue & Yates).
Section 2.2: Detailed exposition of C–I model and inference dichotomies provides clear theoretical foundation.

Introduction: 'A problem in previous studies, including that of Sugawara and Aizawa (2016), is that they analyzed only two datasets and that their categorization of knowledge reasoning is provisional with a weak theoretical background.'

strengths.title: Clear empirical demonstration of independence between readability and question difficulty
strengths.description: The weak correlations (0.025–0.416) across multiple datasets and readability metrics provide empirical evidence that readability and question difficulty are not strongly coupled. This challenges the intuitive assumption that harder-to-read texts lead to harder questions.
evidence: Table 5: Pearson correlations range from 0.025 to 0.416 across datasets and metrics.
Figures 3–4: Visual representation of the 2D space shows clear separation of datasets (e.g., SQuAD difficult-to-read/easy-to-answer, MCTest easy-to-read/difficult-to-answer).
Section 5: 'Although there are weak correlations from 0.025 to 0.416, the results highlight that there is not necessarily a strong correlation between the two values.'

strengths.title: Comprehensive dataset characterization with actionable profiles
strengths.description: The paper provides detailed profiles of six datasets (QA4MRE, MCTest, SQuAD, Who-did-What, MS MARCO, NewsQA) along two dimensions, enabling researchers to select datasets for specific purposes (e.g., curriculum learning, system development).
evidence: Tables 2–4: Frequency distributions of skills, skill counts, and readability metrics for each dataset.

Section 5 & 6: Detailed observations for each dataset (e.g., 'QA4MRE seemed to be the most difficult dataset...', 'MCTest is a good example of an RC dataset that is easy to read but difficult to answer.').
Section 6: Discussion of practical applications (curriculum learning, corpus genre effects, question type implications).

strengths.title: Transparent acknowledgment of methodological limitations
strengths.description: The authors explicitly acknowledge key limitations: inability to evaluate sentence selection competence (A3), readability metrics designed for humans not systems (A2), ambiguity in 'nonsense' classification (A10), and treatment of 'no answer' questions. This transparency strengthens credibility.
evidence: Section 1: 'This means our methodology could not evaluate the competence of looking for sentences that need to be read and answer candidates from the context.'
Section 3.2: 'Nonetheless, because these metrics were proposed for human readability, they do not necessarily correlate with those for RC systems.'
Section 6: 'There were questions for which there were disagreements regarding the decision of nonsense. For example, some questions can be solved by external knowledge without seeing their context.'

strengths.title: Well-structured logical flow from motivation through results to implications
strengths.description: The paper follows a clear logical progression: motivation (Figure 1 examples) → theoretical foundation (C–I model) → metric definition (skills + readability) → annotation methodology → empirical results → dataset profiles → practical implications. Each section builds coherently on prior sections.
evidence: Section 1: Motivation established via concrete examples and problem statement.
Section 2: Related work and psychological theory provide foundation.
Section 3: Metrics defined with explicit theoretical grounding.
Sections 4–5: Methodology and results presented systematically.
Section 6: Discussion connects findings to practical applications (curriculum learning, corpus genre, question type).

concerns.title: Critical assumption (skill count = difficulty) asserted without empirical validation
concerns.description: The paper assumes that the number of required prerequisite skills directly corresponds to question difficulty (A1), stating: 'the more skills that are required to answer a question, the more difficult the question is.' This assumption is foundational to the entire framework but is never empirically validated against system performance or human difficulty judgments.
evidence: Section 1: 'From this observation, we assume that the number of required skills corresponds to the difficulty of a question. This is because each skill corresponds to a function of a system, which has to be equipped with the system.'
The paper provides no evidence that systems with more required skills perform worse, or that humans rate such questions as harder.

Table 3 shows MCTest has average 1.56 skills but is claimed to be 'difficult-to-answer'—this is only moderately higher than SQuAD (1.28) and MS MARCO (1.19), raising questions about the skill-difficulty mapping.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate A1 by: (1) correlating skill count with system performance (accuracy) on these datasets; (2) collecting human difficulty judgments and correlating with skill count; (3) testing whether curriculum learning based on skill count improves system performance. If skill count does not predict difficulty, the framework's utility is compromised.

concerns.title: Readability metrics designed for human comprehension, not RC system performance
concerns.description: The paper acknowledges (A2) that readability metrics from Vajjala & Meurers (2012) were designed for human readability and may not correlate with RC system difficulty. Yet the weak correlations (0.025–0.416) are interpreted as evidence that 'readability does not affect question difficulty,' when they may simply reflect metric mismatch.
evidence: Section 3.2: 'Nonetheless, because these metrics were proposed for human readability, they do not necessarily correlate with those for RC systems. Therefore, in a system analysis, we ideally have to consult various features.'
The paper does not validate that these metrics correlate with actual RC system performance on these datasets.
The weak correlations may be artifacts of using human-oriented metrics rather than evidence of true independence between readability and question difficulty.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate the readability metrics by: (1) correlating them with actual RC system performance (e.g., accuracy of SQuAD-trained models on these datasets); (2) comparing with system-oriented features (e.g., token overlap, entity density, dependency tree depth); (3) testing whether alternative readability metrics (e.g., Pitler & Nenkova 2008) yield different correlations. If human readability metrics do not predict system performance, the framework's applicability to system development is limited.

concerns.title: Sentence selection reliability not quantified; impact on skill annotations unclear
concerns.description: The paper acknowledges (A3) that it 'cannot evaluate the competence of selecting sentences that need to be read to answer questions,' yet this is foundational to the skill annotations. If annotators systematically over- or under-select sentences, skill annotations and readability metrics will be biased. The impact is not quantified.
evidence: Section 1: 'This means our methodology could not evaluate the competence of looking for sentences that need to be read and answer candidates from the context.'
Section 6: 'As mentioned in Section 1, our methodology cannot evaluate the competence of selecting sentences that need to be read to answer questions.'
Table 6 provides only aggregate statistics (average number and distance of sentences); no analysis of inter-annotator agreement on sentence selection.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify sentence selection reliability by: (1) computing inter-annotator agreement specifically for sentence selection (e.g., Jaccard similarity of selected sentence sets); (2) performing sensitivity analysis: re-annotate a subset with different sentence selections and measure impact on skill counts and readability metrics; (3) comparing selected sentences to gold-standard sentence annotations (if available) or to sentences identified by extractive QA systems. This will clarify whether skill annotations are robust to sentence selection variation.

concerns.title: Inter-annotator agreement reported globally; skill-level and dataset-level breakdown missing
concerns.description: The paper reports 90.1% inter-annotator agreement on 62 questions but does not break down agreement by skill or dataset. Some skills (e.g., rare ones like Meta-knowledge with 0–1% frequency) may have very low agreement, while others (e.g., Bridging with 26–69% frequency) may have higher agreement. This variation is not reported.
evidence: Section 5: 'The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions.'
Table 2 shows skill frequencies vary widely (e.g., Meta-knowledge 0–1%, Bridging 26–69%, Punctuation 1–34%).
No per-skill or per-dataset agreement metrics reported; no analysis of which skills are reliably annotated.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report inter-annotator agreement broken down by: (1) skill (compute agreement for each of the 13 skills separately); (2) dataset (compute agreement for each of the 6 datasets); (3) skill frequency (compare agreement for frequent vs. rare skills). Use metrics like Cohen's kappa or Fleiss' kappa to account for chance agreement. This will identify weak points in the taxonomy and guide future refinement.

concerns.title: Sample size (100 questions per dataset) not justified; generalizability not tested
concerns.description: The paper samples 100 questions per dataset, citing Chen et al. (2016) as justification (A7). However, typical RC datasets are much larger (SQuAD ~100K, MS MARCO ~100K). No confidence intervals, bootstrap analysis, or sensitivity analysis is provided to assess whether findings generalize to full datasets.
evidence: Section 4.2: 'For the annotation, we randomly selected 100 questions from each dataset in Table 1. This amount of questions was considered to be sufficient for the analysis of RC datasets as performed by Chen et al. (2016).'
No confidence intervals or bootstrap resampling reported for correlations, skill frequencies, or readability metrics.
No analysis of whether findings hold for different subsets of 100 questions.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Strengthen generalizability claims by: (1) computing 95% confidence intervals for all reported statistics (correlations, skill frequencies, readability metrics); (2) performing bootstrap resampling (e.g., 1000 resamples of 100 questions) to assess stability of findings; (3) testing whether findings hold for larger samples (e.g., 500 or 1000 questions per dataset, if feasible); (4) analyzing whether findings vary by dataset subset (e.g., by topic, source, or question type). This will clarify the robustness of the dataset characterizations.

concerns.title: Pearson correlation assumes linearity; non-linear associations not explored
concerns.description: The paper uses Pearson correlation to measure association between skill count and readability metrics (A6). Pearson assumes a linear relationship; if the relationship is non-linear, monotonic but non-linear, or mediated by dataset-specific factors, Pearson will underestimate or mischaracterize the association.
evidence: Table 5: 'Table 5 presents Pearson's correlation coefficients between the number of required prerequisite skills and each readability metric for all questions of the RC datasets.'
No Spearman rank correlation, Kendall tau, or other non-parametric measures reported.
No scatter plots or residual analysis to assess linearity assumption.
Figures 3–4 show clear clustering by dataset, suggesting dataset-specific relationships not captured by global Pearson correlation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Strengthen correlation analysis by: (1) reporting Spearman rank correlation and Kendall tau in addition to Pearson; (2) computing correlations separately for each dataset (not just globally); (3) visualizing relationships with scatter plots and assessing linearity; (4) testing for non-linear relationships (e.g., polynomial regression, LOESS smoothing); (5) investigating whether dataset-specific factors (genre, curation method, task formulation) mediate the relationship. This will provide a more complete picture of the association between readability and difficulty.

concerns.title: No statistical significance testing for correlations or dataset differences
concerns.description: The paper reports correlations and dataset profiles but does not provide p-values, confidence intervals, or significance tests. It is unclear whether observed differences (e.g., between QA4MRE and MS MARCO) are statistically significant or within noise.
evidence: Table 5: Correlations reported without p-values or significance indicators.
Tables 2–4: Skill frequencies and readability metrics reported without confidence intervals or significance tests.
Section 5: 'QA4MRE seemed to be the most difficult dataset...whereas MS MARCO seemed to be the easiest.' No statistical test of this difference.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Add statistical rigor by: (1) computing p-values for all reported correlations (using permutation tests if assumptions are violated); (2) computing 95% confidence intervals for skill frequencies and readability metrics; (3) performing ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis tests to assess whether datasets differ significantly on skill count and readability; (4) using post-hoc tests (e.g., Tukey HSD) to identify which dataset pairs differ significantly. This will clarify which findings are robust and which are within noise.

concerns.title: Confounding factors (genre, curation, task formulation) not isolated
concerns.description: Datasets differ in multiple ways: genre (narrative vs. expository), curation method (crowdsourced vs. automatic), task formulation (multiple choice vs. span selection), and size. The paper does not isolate the contribution of each factor to observed differences in skill count and readability.
evidence: Section 5: 'MCTest achieved high scores in several skills...These scores seem to be because the MCTest dataset consists of narratives.'
Section 5: 'Who-did-What achieved the highest score for ellipsis. This is because the questions of Who-did-What are automatically generated from articles not used as context.'
Section 6: 'Attention should be paid to the genre of corpus used to construct a dataset. Expository documents like news articles tend to require factorial understanding.'
No systematic analysis of how genre, curation method, or task formulation independently affect skill count and readability.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Isolate confounding factors by: (1) grouping datasets by genre (narrative vs. expository) and comparing skill/readability profiles; (2) grouping by curation method (crowdsourced vs. automatic) and comparing; (3) grouping by task formulation (multiple choice vs. span selection) and comparing; (4) using regression analysis to estimate the independent contribution of each factor to skill count and readability, controlling for others. This will clarify which dataset differences are due to inherent properties vs. methodological choices.

concerns.title: Curriculum learning application is speculative; no empirical validation
concerns.description: Section 6 proposes using the framework for curriculum learning (ordering datasets by difficulty for stepwise system development), but provides no empirical evidence that this approach improves system performance. The claim is speculative.
evidence: Section 6: 'One example for the development of an RC system is that it should be built to solve an easy-to-read and easy-to-answer dataset. The next step is to improve the system so that it can solve an easy-to-read and difficult-to-answer dataset. Finally, only after it can solve such dataset should the system be applied to a difficult-to-read and difficult-to-answer dataset.'
No experiments showing that curriculum learning based on this framework improves performance compared to standard training.
No comparison with other curriculum learning strategies or dataset ordering schemes.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate the curriculum learning application by: (1) training RC systems (e.g., SQuAD-based models) on datasets ordered by the proposed difficulty metric and measuring learning curves; (2) comparing with random dataset ordering and other curriculum learning strategies; (3) testing whether the proposed ordering improves final performance or convergence speed. This would provide empirical support for the practical utility of the framework.

concerns.title: Skill taxonomy refinement not empirically compared to prior taxonomy
concerns.description: The paper claims the 13-skill taxonomy is more theoretically grounded than the prior 10-skill taxonomy (C3), but provides no empirical comparison. No evidence that the new taxonomy better predicts system performance, human difficulty judgments, or has higher inter-annotator agreement.
evidence: Section 1: 'A problem in previous studies, including that of Sugawara and Aizawa (2016), is that they analyzed only two datasets and that their categorization of knowledge reasoning is provisional with a weak theoretical background.'
Section 3.1: 'By refining Sugawara et al. (2017)'s ten reading comprehension skills, we reorganized thirteen prerequisite skills in total.'
No comparison of annotation consistency, predictive power, or utility between old and new taxonomies.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Empirically validate the taxonomy refinement by: (1) re-annotating a subset of questions using the old 10-skill taxonomy and comparing inter-annotator agreement; (2) testing whether the new taxonomy better predicts system performance (e.g., via regression analysis); (3) collecting human difficulty judgments and testing whether the new taxonomy better predicts human judgments; (4) analyzing whether the new taxonomy reduces ambiguity in skill definitions (e.g., by comparing annotation disagreements). This would provide evidence that the refinement is not just theoretically motivated but empirically beneficial.

concerns.title: Framework utility for system development not empirically demonstrated
concerns.description: The paper claims the two-class framework (skills + readability) characterizes RC datasets 'more comprehensively' than superficial categories (C4), but provides no empirical evidence that systems trained with knowledge of these metrics perform better or that the framework guides system development.
evidence: Section 1: 'We adopt two classes of evaluation metrics to show the qualitative features of RC datasets.'
Section 7: 'Our annotation highlights the characteristics of the datasets and provides a valuable guide for the construction of new datasets and the development of RC systems.'
No experiments showing that systems informed by this framework outperform systems trained without this knowledge.
No case studies of dataset construction or system development guided by the framework.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Demonstrate framework utility by: (1) training RC systems on datasets selected using the framework (e.g., curriculum learning) and measuring performance; (2) constructing a new RC dataset using the framework to guide design choices and evaluating its quality; (3) comparing system performance when trained with vs. without knowledge of the framework; (4) conducting user studies with dataset designers to assess whether the framework guides design decisions. This would provide evidence that the framework is not just descriptive but prescriptive.

concerns.title: Dataset exclusion rationale may introduce bias; excluded datasets not analyzed
concerns.description: The paper excludes CNN/Daily Mail, CBTest, and LAMBADA from analysis (Section 4.2) with stated reasons (anonymization, language modeling task, machine-formatted text). However, these exclusions may bias the sample toward higher-quality datasets and limit generalizability.
evidence: Section 4.2: 'CNN/Daily Mail (Hermann et al., 2015) is anonymized and contains some errors (Chen et al., 2016), so it did not seem to be suitable for annotation. We considered CBTest (Hill et al., 2016) to be for language modeling tasks rather than RC task and excluded it. LAMBADA (Paperno et al., 2016)'s texts are formatted for machine reading, and all tokens are lowercased, which seemingly prevents inferences based on proper nouns.'
CNN/Daily Mail is one of the largest RC datasets; excluding it limits the sample.
No analysis of whether findings would change if these datasets were included.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Strengthen the analysis by: (1) providing more detailed justification for exclusions (e.g., quantifying the impact of anonymization on CNN/Daily Mail); (2) attempting to annotate at least a subset of excluded datasets to test whether findings generalize; (3) discussing how exclusions may bias the sample (e.g., toward higher-quality datasets); (4) analyzing whether the six included datasets are representative of the broader landscape of RC datasets. This would clarify the scope and limitations of the study.

concerns.title: Readability metrics applied only to selected sentences; full-document readability not assessed
concerns.description: The paper applies readability metrics only to annotator-selected sentences (Section 3.2), not to full documents. This may not reflect the actual readability difficulty experienced by systems, which must process entire documents.
evidence: Section 3.2: 'We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions.'
Section 6: 'Analyses were performed in two ways: for each question, we counted the number of required sentences and their distance.'
Table 6 shows average 1.04–1.18 sentences per question; readability metrics computed on such small samples may not be stable.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Strengthen readability assessment by: (1) computing readability metrics on full documents and comparing with sentence-level metrics; (2) analyzing how document-level readability correlates with question difficulty; (3) testing whether findings change if readability is computed on different sentence selections (e.g., all sentences, first N sentences, or sentences containing answer entities). This would clarify whether the weak correlations are due to sentence-level analysis or reflect true independence.

comparable_works.relevance: Directly prior work on prerequisite skills for RC; this paper refines the 10-skill taxonomy to 13 skills
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: Both use prerequisite skills to characterize RC datasets. Difference: Sugawara et al. analyzed only 2 datasets (MCTest); this paper analyzes 6 datasets. Sugawara et al.'s taxonomy lacked theoretical grounding; this paper grounds it in psychology and entailment theory.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 1, Introduction; Section 3.1

comparable_works.relevance: Theoretical foundation for the two-class framework (strategic/skilled comprehension + text ease of processing)
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: Both adopt McNamara & Magliano's distinction between comprehension difficulty and text readability. Difference: McNamara & Magliano focus on human comprehension; this paper applies the framework to RC datasets and systems.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 2.2, Reading Comprehension in Psychology; Section 3

comparable_works.relevance: Source of the 10 readability metrics used in the paper
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: Both use linguistic features for readability assessment. Difference: Vajjala & Meurers focus on second-language acquisition; this paper applies metrics to RC datasets. The paper acknowledges that human readability metrics may not correlate with RC system difficulty.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 3.2, Readability Metrics

comparable_works.relevance: Identified quality issues in CNN/Daily Mail dataset; justifies the need for dataset evaluation metrics
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: Both assess RC dataset quality. Difference: Chen et al. focus on identifying unsolvable/nonsense questions; this paper provides a systematic framework for characterizing datasets along two dimensions.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 1, Introduction; Section 4.2

comparable_works.relevance: Construction-Integration (C–I) model provides theoretical foundation for the two-class framework
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: Both use C–I model to understand text comprehension. Difference: Kintsch focuses on human cognition; this paper applies the model to RC dataset evaluation.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 2.2, Reading Comprehension in Psychology

comparable_works.relevance: Textual entailment framework used to ground the knowledge reasoning skills in the taxonomy
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: Both use entailment phenomena to classify inference types. Difference: Dagan et al. focus on entailment recognition; this paper applies entailment concepts to RC skill taxonomy.
comparable_works.source_trace: Section 1, Introduction; Section 3.1

uncertainty_flags: Skill count as difficulty proxy: The foundational assumption (A1) that skill count = difficulty is asserted but not empirically validated. If this assumption is invalid, the entire framework's utility is compromised.

Readability metric applicability: Metrics designed for human readability (A2) may not reflect RC system difficulty. Weak correlations may be artifacts of metric mismatch rather than true independence.
Sentence selection reliability: The inability to evaluate sentence selection competence (A3) is acknowledged but not quantified. Impact on skill annotations is unclear.
Inter-annotator agreement generalization: Global agreement (90.1% on 62 questions) may not generalize to all skills or datasets. Skill-level and dataset-level breakdown is missing.
Sample size representativeness: 100 questions per dataset is small relative to typical dataset sizes. Generalizability to full datasets not tested; no confidence intervals provided.
Correlation linearity assumption: Pearson correlation assumes linearity (A6); non-linear or dataset-specific relationships not explored.
Statistical significance: No p-values or significance tests reported. Unclear whether observed differences are statistically significant.
Confounding factors: Dataset differences in genre, curation, task formulation not isolated. Causal mechanisms unclear.
Curriculum learning validation: Proposed curriculum learning application is speculative; no empirical evidence that it improves system performance.
Taxonomy refinement validation: New 13-skill taxonomy not empirically compared to prior 10-skill taxonomy. No evidence of improved predictive power or reliability.
Framework utility: Two-class framework claimed to be more comprehensive, but no empirical demonstration that systems informed by it perform better.
Dataset exclusion bias: Excluded datasets (CNN/Daily Mail, CBTest, LAMBADA) may bias sample toward higher-quality datasets. Impact on generalizability unclear.
Readability metric scope: Metrics applied only to selected sentences, not full documents. May not reflect actual document readability.
External knowledge in questions: Ambiguity in identifying questions solvable by external knowledge (A10) affects 'nonsense' classification and dataset characterization.
alternative_interpretations: Weak correlations as metric mismatch: The weak correlations (0.025–0.416) between readability and skill count may not indicate true independence but rather reflect the mismatch between human-oriented readability metrics and RC system difficulty. If system-oriented metrics were used, stronger correlations might emerge.

Skill count as proxy for system architecture requirements: Rather than difficulty, skill count may reflect the number of system components or functions required. A question requiring 5 skills may not be harder but may require a more complex system architecture.

Dataset differences as methodological artifacts: Observed differences between datasets (e.g., QA4MRE difficult, MS MARCO easy) may reflect differences in curation method, genre, or task formulation rather than inherent difficulty. Isolating these factors is necessary to interpret dataset profiles.

Curriculum learning as dataset ordering: The proposed curriculum learning application may be better framed as dataset ordering for transfer learning rather than curriculum learning in the traditional sense (easy-to-hard progression). The paper does not validate that the proposed ordering is optimal.

Skill taxonomy as system capability checklist: The 13-skill taxonomy may be better interpreted as a checklist of system capabilities required to solve questions, rather than a measure of question difficulty. This interpretation is more aligned with the paper's methodology.

Readability as text complexity, not difficulty: Readability metrics measure text complexity (vocabulary, syntax), not difficulty for RC systems. A complex text may be easy to answer if the question targets a simple fact, and vice versa.

Genre effects confounded with readability: The observation that MCTest (narrative) is easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer may reflect genre effects (narratives are inherently easier to read) rather than a fundamental independence between readability and difficulty.

Sample bias toward high-quality datasets: The exclusion of CNN/Daily Mail (large, noisy) and inclusion of high-quality datasets (SQuAD, NewsQA) may bias the sample. Findings may not generalize to lower-quality datasets.
transparency_notes: The paper explicitly acknowledges key limitations: inability to evaluate sentence selection competence, readability metrics designed for humans not systems, ambiguity in 'nonsense' classification, and treatment of 'no answer' questions. This transparency is commendable.
The paper does not report statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or per-skill inter-annotator agreement. These omissions limit the ability to assess robustness of findings.

The paper does not provide code or detailed annotation guidelines, limiting reproducibility. The authors state 'We will make available the analysis of RC datasets on basic features as much as possible,' but it is unclear what will be released.
The paper does not discuss potential biases in annotator selection, training, or compensation. Annotator demographics and expertise are not reported.
The paper does not discuss how disagreements between annotators were resolved. Were disagreements adjudicated by a third annotator, or were they resolved by majority vote?
The paper does not provide examples of annotated questions, making it difficult to assess the quality of annotations or the clarity of skill definitions.
The paper does not discuss the computational cost of annotation or the time required per question. This information would be useful for future annotation studies.
The paper does not discuss potential conflicts of interest or funding sources. It is unclear whether the authors have any stake in the datasets or systems analyzed.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper's main contribution—a two-class framework for characterizing RC datasets along readability and prerequisite skills dimensions—is novel in its systematic application to six datasets and its explicit grounding in psychology and entailment theory. However, novelty does not guarantee validity. The framework's utility depends on empirical validation of key assumptions (skill count = difficulty, readability metrics reflect system difficulty) and demonstration of practical benefits (curriculum learning, system development guidance). The paper provides limited evidence on these fronts.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If skill count empirically predicts system performance (e.g., via regression analysis), the framework would be more credible as a difficulty measure.
If readability metrics correlate with actual RC system performance on these datasets, the framework would be more applicable to system development.
If curriculum learning based on the proposed dataset ordering improves system performance compared to random ordering, the practical utility of the framework would be demonstrated.
If the 13-skill taxonomy has higher inter-annotator agreement and better predictive power than the prior 10-skill taxonomy, the refinement would be empirically justified.
If the framework guides the construction of new RC datasets that are more useful for system development, its practical impact would be demonstrated.
If the framework is adopted by other researchers and used to characterize additional datasets, its utility and generalizability would be validated.
If the paper provides detailed annotation guidelines and examples, enabling other researchers to replicate and extend the work, its scientific impact would be enhanced.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper refines Sugawara et al. (2017)'s 10-skill taxonomy to 13 skills with explicit grounding in psychology and entailment theory. This is an incremental improvement over prior work, not a fundamental innovation. The refinement is theoretically motivated but not empirically validated against the prior taxonomy.
evidence: Section 1: 'A problem in previous studies, including that of Sugawara and Aizawa (2016), is that they analyzed only two datasets and that their categorization of knowledge reasoning is provisional with a weak theoretical background.'
Section 3.1: 'By refining Sugawara et al. (2017)'s ten reading comprehension skills, we reorganized thirteen prerequisite skills in total.'
No empirical comparison of the new vs. old taxonomy.
uncertainty_flags: Novelty of taxonomy refinement is limited; the core skills are similar to prior work.
Theoretical grounding is asserted but not empirically validated.
No evidence that the new taxonomy is more useful or reliable than the prior taxonomy.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper systematically annotates and characterizes six RC datasets along two dimensions (readability and prerequisite skills). This is more comprehensive than prior work (Sugawara et al. analyzed 2 datasets). The systematic comparison and dataset profiles are novel contributions.
evidence: Section 4.2: 'For the annotation, we randomly selected 100 questions from each dataset in Table 1.'
Tables 2–5: Comprehensive characterization of six datasets.
Section 5 & 6: Detailed dataset profiles and comparative analysis.
uncertainty_flags: Novelty is primarily in scope (6 datasets vs. 2 prior) rather than methodology.
Sample size (100 questions per dataset) is small; generalizability unclear.
Findings are descriptive rather than prescriptive; limited guidance for system development.

novelty_lenses.lens: Two-class evaluation framework for RC datasets
novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper proposes a two-class framework (readability + prerequisite skills) for evaluating RC datasets, grounded in McNamara & Magliano (2009)'s theory of text comprehension. This is a novel application of psychological theory to RC dataset evaluation, but the framework is not empirically validated for practical utility.
evidence: Section 3: 'Based on McNamara and Magliano (2009)'s depiction of text comprehension, we adopted two classes for the evaluation of RC datasets: prerequisite skills and readability.'
Section 1: 'We adopt two classes of evaluation metrics to show the qualitative features of RC datasets.'
No empirical demonstration that the framework guides system development or improves performance.
uncertainty_flags: Framework is theoretically motivated but not empirically validated.
Utility for system development is speculative; no case studies or experiments provided.
Readability metrics may not reflect RC system difficulty; applicability unclear.

novelty_lenses.lens: Empirical finding: weak correlation between readability and difficulty
novelty_lenses.rationale: The empirical finding that readability and question difficulty are weakly correlated (0.025–0.416) is interesting and challenges the intuitive assumption that harder-to-read texts lead to harder questions. However, the finding may be an artifact of metric mismatch (human-oriented readability metrics vs. RC system difficulty) rather than a fundamental insight.
evidence: Table 5: Pearson correlations range from 0.025 to 0.416.
Figures 3–4: Visual demonstration of weak correlation.
Section 5: 'Although there are weak correlations from 0.025 to 0.416, the results highlight that there is not necessarily a strong correlation between the two values.'
uncertainty_flags: Weak correlations may reflect metric mismatch rather than true independence.
No validation that readability metrics correlate with RC system performance.
Confounding factors (genre, curation, task formulation) not isolated; causal mechanisms unclear.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper makes solid empirical contributions (systematic annotation of 6 datasets, comprehensive characterization, weak correlation finding) with generally sound methodology. However, critical assumptions are not empirically validated (skill count = difficulty, readability metrics reflect system difficulty), and the practical utility of the framework is not demonstrated. The paper's logical structure is coherent, but the gap between theoretical motivation and empirical validation limits confidence in the main claims. The work is publishable as a dataset characterization study but requires additional validation for claims about framework utility and curriculum learning applications. Confidence is moderate-to-high for descriptive findings (dataset profiles, correlations) but lower for prescriptive claims (framework utility, curriculum learning).

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper presents a systematic empirical study of six reading comprehension datasets using two evaluation dimensions: prerequisite skills (13-category taxonomy) and readability metrics (10 linguistic features). The core contribution is demonstrating weak correlations (0.025–0.416) between readability and question difficulty, challenging the assumption that difficult-to-read texts necessarily yield difficult questions. The work is grounded in psychological theory (Construction-Integration model, McNamara & Magliano 2009) and entailment theory. Methodologically, the paper conducts manual annotation of 600 questions (100 per dataset) with reported inter-annotator agreement of 90.1% on a 62-question sample. The main findings characterize six datasets along the two dimensions and propose curriculum learning applications. Critical evaluation reveals significant methodological limitations: (1) sample size (100 questions per dataset) may not represent full distributions; (2) readability metrics designed for human comprehension may not reflect RC system difficulty; (3) the 13-skill taxonomy's theoretical grounding is asserted but not empirically validated against prior work; (4) correlation analysis uses only Pearson's coefficient without exploring non-linear relationships or statistical significance testing; (5) sentence selection reliability is acknowledged as unvalidated; (6) dataset exclusion rationale may introduce bias. The paper makes incremental contributions to dataset characterization but lacks empirical validation of its core assumptions and framework utility.
logical_argument_graph: Premise: McNamara & Magliano (2009) propose two aspects of text comprehension: strategic/skilled comprehension and text ease of processing.
Premise: Kintsch (1993) and McNamara & Magliano (2009) distinguish between bridging (retrieved) and elaboration (generated) inferences.
Premise: Dagan et al. (2013) and LoBue & Yates (2011) provide classification of entailment phenomena.
Inference: These psychological and NLP theories can be synthesized into a 13-skill taxonomy for RC evaluation.
Premise: Vajjala & Meurers (2012) identify 10 linguistic features affecting human readability.
Inference: These features can be applied to RC dataset evaluation.
Premise: Sugawara et al. (2017) propose that skill count correlates with question difficulty.
Assumption A1: The number of required prerequisite skills directly corresponds to question difficulty.
Inference: If A1 holds, weak correlations between skill count and readability metrics imply independence of readability and question difficulty.
Empirical Finding: Pearson correlations between skill count and readability metrics range from 0.025–0.416 across six datasets.
Conclusion C1: Readability does not directly correlate with question difficulty.
Observation: MCTest has low readability scores but moderate skill requirements.
Conclusion C2: Easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer datasets are constructible.
Observation: Different datasets exhibit distinct profiles in the readability-skill space.
Conclusion C5: Dataset-specific profiles characterize RC dataset quality.
Implication: Curriculum learning can order datasets by difficulty for stepwise system development.
Caveat: This implication is speculative and not empirically validated.

identified_claims.claim_label: Weak correlation between readability and question difficulty
identified_claims.claim_text: Readability of RC dataset texts does not directly correlate with question difficulty; correlations range from 0.025–0.416 across datasets
evidence: Table 5 presents Pearson's correlation coefficients between the number of required prerequisite skills and each readability metric for all questions of the RC datasets. Although there are weak correlations from 0.025 to 0.416, the results highlight that there is not necessarily a strong correlation between the two values.
Figure 3 shows trends of datasets: QA4MRE was relatively difficult both to read and to answer, and SQuAD was difficult to read but easy to answer.
This leads to the following two insights. First, the readability of RC datasets does not directly affect the difficulty of their questions.
uncertainty_flags: Correlation strength interpretation depends on domain conventions; 0.025–0.416 range spans weak to moderate, but no formal threshold for 'direct correlation' is defined
Sample size per dataset is 100 questions; generalizability to larger samples or other datasets not empirically tested
Readability metrics applied only to sentences selected by annotators as necessary; does not reflect full document readability
Pearson correlation assumes linear relationship; non-linear associations not explored
No statistical significance testing reported; unclear if correlations are significantly different from zero or from each other
Confounding factors (dataset size, curation method, genre, task formulation) vary across datasets; causal mechanisms not isolated

identified_claims.claim_label: Easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer datasets are constructible
identified_claims.claim_text: It is possible to construct RC datasets that are easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer, exemplified by MCTest
identified_claims.section_anchor: Section 1, Introduction; Section 5, Results; Section 6, Discussion
evidence: In the second example from MCTest (Richardson et al., 2013), the document is written for children and is easy to read, but the question requires reading multiple sentences and a combination of several skills, such as understanding of causal relations, coreference resolution, and complementing ellipsis.
MCTest is a good example of an RC dataset that is easy to read but difficult to answer. The corpus' genre (i.e., narrative) seems to reflect the trend of required skills for the questions.
Table 4 shows MCTest had the lowest readability scores; Table 3 shows MCTest questions required average 1.56 skills (moderate difficulty).
uncertainty_flags: MCTest is a single exemplar; no systematic construction methodology provided for replicating this property
Difficulty assessment relies on annotator judgment of prerequisite skills; no independent validation against system performance or human difficulty judgments
Genre (narrative vs. expository) is confounded with readability; causal mechanism not isolated
Sample size (100 questions) may not be representative of full MCTest dataset characteristics
Average skill count (1.56) is not substantially higher than SQuAD (1.28) or MS MARCO (1.19); claim of 'difficult-to-answer' is relative and not absolute
No comparison of MCTest difficulty to other datasets using statistical significance testing

identified_claims.claim_label: Refined 13-skill taxonomy provides theoretically grounded classification
identified_claims.claim_text: A reorganized taxonomy of 13 prerequisite skills (from prior 10-skill work) provides more theoretically grounded classification than previous studies, grounded in psychology (C–I model, bridging/elaboration) and entailment theory
evidence: We reorganized the category of knowledge reasoning in terms of textual entailment and human text comprehension. In research on textual entailment, several methodologies have been proposed for precise analysis of entailment phenomena (Dagan et al., 2013; LoBue and Yates, 2011). In psychology research, Kintsch (1993) proposed dichotomies for the classification of human inferences: retrieved versus generated. In addition, McNamara and Magliano (2009) proposed a similar distinction for inferences: bridging versus elaboration.
Skills 8–10 (Ellipsis, Bridging, Elaboration) are explicitly grounded in psychology and entailment literature.

A problem in previous studies, including that of Sugawara and Aizawa (2016), is that they analyzed only two datasets and that their categorization of knowledge reasoning is provisional with a weak theoretical background.
uncertainty_flags: Theoretical grounding is asserted but not formally validated; no empirical test of whether the 13-skill taxonomy better predicts system performance than prior 10-skill taxonomy
Mapping between psychology concepts (bridging/elaboration) and NLP entailment phenomena is conceptual; no formal alignment procedure described
Inter-annotator agreement (90.1% on 62 questions) is reported globally but not broken down by skill; some skills may have lower reliability
No comparison of annotation consistency between old and new taxonomies
The claim that the new taxonomy is 'more theoretically grounded' is comparative but no quantitative measure of theoretical grounding is provided
Skills 1–7 and 11–13 are less explicitly grounded in the cited theories; their theoretical justification is less clear

identified_claims.claim_label: Two-class metric framework characterizes RC datasets more comprehensively
identified_claims.claim_text: Two classes of metrics—prerequisite skills and readability—together characterize RC dataset quality more comprehensively than existing superficial categorizations (e.g., question type, answer type)
evidence: In these situations, it is difficult to assess systems accurately. As Norvig (1989) stated, questions easy for humans often turn out to be difficult for systems.

However, a current problem is that most RC datasets are presented only with superficial categories, such as question types (e.g., what, where, and who) and answer types (e.g., numeric, location, and person).
We adopt two classes of evaluation metrics to show the qualitative features of RC datasets.
uncertainty_flags: Comprehensiveness is asserted but not quantitatively measured; no metric for comparing framework expressiveness
No empirical demonstration that systems trained with knowledge of these two classes perform better than systems trained without
Readability metrics are borrowed from second-language acquisition literature; applicability to RC system development not validated
Framework does not address other potentially relevant dimensions (e.g., answer type, question type, context length, answer span position)
No comparison with alternative frameworks for dataset characterization
The claim that existing categorizations are 'superficial' is not formally justified; question type and answer type may capture important variance

identified_claims.claim_label: Dataset-specific profiles characterize six RC datasets
identified_claims.claim_text: Different RC datasets exhibit distinct profiles: QA4MRE is difficult on both dimensions; SQuAD is difficult-to-read but easy-to-answer; MCTest is easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer; MS MARCO is easiest; Who-did-What and NewsQA occupy intermediate positions
evidence: QA4MRE seemed to be the most difficult dataset among the RC datasets we analyzed, whereas MS MARCO seemed to be the easiest.
SQuAD was difficult to read along with QA4MRE but relatively easy to answer compared to other datasets.
MCTest is a good example of an RC dataset that is easy to read but difficult to answer.
Table 3: QA4MRE average 3.25 skills; MCTest 1.56; SQuAD 1.28; MS MARCO 1.19.
Table 4: SQuAD and QA4MRE achieved the highest scores in most metrics; MCTest had the lowest scores.
uncertainty_flags: Profiles are based on 100 questions per dataset; may not represent full dataset distributions
Difficulty rankings are relative to this sample; absolute difficulty thresholds not defined
Confounding factors: dataset size, curation method, genre, and task formulation all vary; isolating contribution of each unclear
No statistical significance testing of differences between datasets
MCTest's 'difficult-to-answer' label is questionable given average skill count of 1.56 (lower than QA4MRE 3.25 and Who-did-What 2.43)
Profiles may not generalize to full datasets or to future RC systems with different architectures

strengths.title: Systematic annotation study with transparent inter-annotator agreement reporting
strengths.description: The paper conducts manual annotation of 600 questions across six datasets with reported inter-annotator agreement of 90.1% on a 62-question sample. This provides empirical grounding for the annotation procedure and demonstrates effort toward reproducibility.
evidence: The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions.
Annotation procedure is clearly described in Section 4.1, including allowance for multiple labeling and handling of unsolvable questions.
Annotation results are made publicly available (stated in contributions).

strengths.title: Grounding in established psychological and NLP theory
strengths.description: The framework is explicitly grounded in McNamara & Magliano (2009)'s Construction-Integration model, Kintsch's (1993) inference classification, and entailment theory (Dagan et al., 2013). This provides theoretical justification for the two-class metric approach and distinguishes the work from purely empirical categorizations.
evidence: Our two classes of metrics are based on McNamara and Magliano (2009)'s analysis of human text comprehension in psychology.
We reorganized the category of knowledge reasoning in terms of textual entailment and human text comprehension.
Skills 8–10 (Ellipsis, Bridging, Elaboration) are explicitly grounded in psychology and entailment literature.

strengths.title: Clear demonstration of independence between readability and question difficulty
strengths.description: The paper provides concrete examples (SQuAD vs. MCTest) and empirical evidence (correlation coefficients 0.025–0.416) showing that readability and question difficulty are not strongly coupled. This challenges a common implicit assumption in RC dataset design and is useful for practitioners.
evidence: Figure 1 provides two concrete examples illustrating the independence of readability and difficulty.
Figure 3 and Figure 4 visually demonstrate the scatter of datasets in the readability-skill space.
Table 5 quantifies weak correlations across multiple readability metrics.
