strengths.title: Comprehensive coverage of six diverse RC datasets
strengths.description: The study analyzes six datasets with different characteristics (QA4MRE, MCTest, SQuAD, Who-did-What, MS MARCO, NewsQA), providing comparative insights across different dataset designs, genres, and curation methods.
evidence: Section 4.2 specifies the six datasets and their characteristics.
Tables 2–4 provide comparative statistics across all six datasets.
Section 5 and 6 discuss dataset-specific observations and profiles.

strengths.title: Acknowledgment of methodological limitations
strengths.description: The authors explicitly acknowledge several limitations: inability to evaluate sentence selection competence, ambiguity in identifying 'nonsense' questions, difficulty handling 'no answer' questions, and the fact that readability metrics are human-oriented rather than system-oriented. This transparency supports reproducibility and guides future work.
evidence: As mentioned in Section 1, our methodology cannot evaluate the competence of selecting sentences that need to be read to answer questions.
Nonetheless, because these metrics were proposed for human readability, they do not necessarily correlate with those for RC systems.
There were questions for which there were disagreements regarding the decision of nonsense.
Annotators reported that the prerequisite skills did not easily treat questions whose answer was 'none of the above' in QA4MRE.

strengths.title: Practical applicability to curriculum learning
strengths.description: The paper proposes a concrete application of the framework to curriculum learning, suggesting that datasets can be ordered by difficulty (along both readability and skill dimensions) for stepwise system development. This provides actionable guidance for practitioners.
evidence: One example for the development of an RC system is that it should be built to solve an easy-to-read and easy-to-answer dataset. The next step is to improve the system so that it can solve an easy-to-read and difficult-to-answer dataset.

Such datasets can be placed in a continuum based on the grades of the metrics and applied to each step of the development, like in curriculum learning (Bengio et al., 2009) and transfer learning (Pan and Yang, 2010).

concerns.title: Sample size (100 questions per dataset) may not represent full dataset distributions
concerns.description: The paper annotates only 100 questions per dataset, which is 10% of typical dataset sizes. While the authors cite Chen et al. (2016) as precedent, no confidence intervals, bootstrap analysis, or sensitivity analysis is provided to assess how representative this sample is of the full dataset.
evidence: For the annotation, we randomly selected 100 questions from each dataset in Table 1. This amount of questions was considered to be sufficient for the analysis of RC datasets as performed by Chen et al. (2016).
No confidence intervals or bootstrap resampling reported for dataset-level statistics.
No sensitivity analysis showing how results change with different sample sizes.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct bootstrap resampling to estimate confidence intervals for dataset-level statistics (e.g., average skill count, readability metrics). Report 95% CIs for all reported means and correlations. Alternatively, annotate a larger sample (e.g., 200–300 questions per dataset) to increase representativeness.

concerns.title: Pearson correlation assumes linearity; non-linear relationships not explored
concerns.description: Table 5 reports only Pearson correlation coefficients between skill count and readability metrics. Pearson correlation assumes a linear relationship. If the relationship is non-linear, monotonic but non-linear, or mediated by dataset-specific factors, Pearson correlation will underestimate or mischaracterize the association. Spearman rank correlation, Kendall's tau, or non-parametric methods should be reported.
evidence: Table 5 presents Pearson's correlation coefficients between the number of required prerequisite skills and each readability metric for all questions of the RC datasets.
No alternative correlation measures (Spearman, Kendall) reported.
No scatter plots or residual analysis to assess linearity assumption.
Figures 3 and 4 suggest potential non-linear patterns (e.g., clustering in QA4MRE, MCTest, SQuAD).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report Spearman rank correlation and Kendall's tau in addition to Pearson correlation. Create scatter plots with fitted curves (e.g., LOWESS) to visualize non-linear relationships. Conduct dataset-specific correlation analysis to identify whether relationships vary by dataset.

concerns.title: No statistical significance testing reported for correlations or dataset differences
concerns.description: The paper reports correlation coefficients and dataset statistics but does not provide p-values, confidence intervals, or significance tests. It is unclear whether observed correlations are significantly different from zero or whether differences between datasets are statistically significant.
evidence: Table 5 presents correlation coefficients without p-values or significance indicators.
No ANOVA or post-hoc tests comparing dataset-level statistics.
No statement of statistical significance for any reported findings.
Claim that correlations are 'weak' is based on magnitude alone, not statistical testing.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report p-values and 95% confidence intervals for all correlation coefficients in Table 5. Conduct one-way ANOVA to test whether dataset-level statistics (average skill count, readability metrics) differ significantly across datasets. Report effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d) for pairwise comparisons.

concerns.title: Inter-annotator agreement (90.1%) reported globally but not broken down by skill or dataset
concerns.description: The paper reports overall inter-annotator agreement of 90.1% on 62 questions but does not provide skill-specific or dataset-specific agreement rates. Some skills (e.g., rare skills like Meta-knowledge or Analogy) may have much lower agreement, undermining the reliability of those skill annotations.
evidence: The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions.
No breakdown of agreement by skill type or dataset.
Table 2 shows that some skills are rare (e.g., Meta-knowledge: 0–1% frequency; Analogy: 0–7% frequency), suggesting potential agreement issues for rare skills.
No Cohen's kappa or other inter-rater reliability measure reported.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's kappa or Fleiss' kappa) broken down by skill and dataset. Identify skills with low agreement and discuss potential causes. Consider merging or redefining low-agreement skills. Report agreement for the full 600-question set, not just the 62-question sample.

concerns.title: Readability metrics applied only to selected sentences, not full documents
concerns.description: The paper applies readability metrics only to sentences annotators identified as necessary for answering questions, not to full documents. This may bias readability scores and affect correlations with skill count. The impact of this choice on the main findings is not quantified.
evidence: We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions.
No analysis of how full-document readability would differ from selected-sentence readability.
Table 6 shows average number and distance of selected sentences, but no comparison of readability metrics computed on full documents vs. selected sentences.
This methodological choice is acknowledged but not validated.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute readability metrics on both selected sentences and full documents. Compare the two sets of metrics and report correlations with skill count for both. Conduct sensitivity analysis showing how results change if full-document readability is used instead of selected-sentence readability.

concerns.title: Sentence selection reliability is acknowledged but not quantified
concerns.description: The authors acknowledge that they cannot evaluate the competence of selecting sentences necessary to answer questions (Section 1 and Section 6). This is a critical assumption (A3) because if annotators systematically over- or under-select sentences, skill annotations and readability metrics will be biased. The impact of this limitation is not quantified.
evidence: As mentioned in Section 1, our methodology cannot evaluate the competence of selecting sentences that need to be read to answer questions.
Competence of selecting necessary sentences: As mentioned in Section 1, our methodology cannot evaluate the competence of selecting sentences that need to be read to answer questions.
No inter-annotator agreement reported specifically for sentence selection.
No analysis of how variation in sentence selection affects skill annotations.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct inter-annotator agreement analysis specifically for sentence selection (e.g., Jaccard similarity of selected sentence sets). Perform sensitivity analysis: re-annotate a subset of questions with different sentence selections and measure how skill annotations change. Report the impact on correlations with readability metrics.

concerns.title: Theoretical grounding of 13-skill taxonomy asserted but not empirically validated
concerns.description: The paper claims that the 13-skill taxonomy is 'more theoretically grounded' than the prior 10-skill taxonomy, but provides no empirical evidence. No comparison of predictive power, inter-annotator agreement, or utility for system development is provided. The mapping between psychology concepts (bridging/elaboration) and NLP entailment phenomena is conceptual, not formal.
evidence: A problem in previous studies, including that of Sugawara and Aizawa (2016), is that they analyzed only two datasets and that their categorization of knowledge reasoning is provisional with a weak theoretical background.
No empirical comparison of the 13-skill taxonomy with the prior 10-skill taxonomy.
No validation that the new taxonomy better predicts system performance or human difficulty judgments.
Mapping between psychology and NLP concepts is described conceptually but not formalized.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct a comparative study: annotate a subset of questions with both the old 10-skill and new 13-skill taxonomies. Compare inter-annotator agreement, skill frequency distributions, and predictive power for system performance. Report quantitative evidence that the new taxonomy is superior.

concerns.title: Curriculum learning application is speculative and not empirically validated
concerns.description: Section 6 proposes using the framework for curriculum learning (ordering datasets by difficulty for stepwise system development), but provides no empirical validation. No experiments are reported showing that systems trained on datasets ordered by this framework learn better than systems trained on randomly ordered datasets.
evidence: One example for the development of an RC system is that it should be built to solve an easy-to-read and easy-to-answer dataset. The next step is to improve the system so that it can solve an easy-to-read and difficult-to-answer dataset.
No experiments reported testing curriculum learning with this framework.
No comparison with other curriculum learning strategies.
This application is presented as a suggestion, not a validated contribution.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct curriculum learning experiments: train RC systems on datasets ordered by the proposed framework and compare learning curves with systems trained on randomly ordered datasets or other curriculum strategies. Report whether the proposed ordering improves convergence speed or final performance.

concerns.title: Dataset exclusion rationale may introduce bias toward higher-quality datasets
concerns.description: The paper excludes CNN/Daily Mail (due to errors), CBTest (deemed language modeling rather than RC), and LAMBADA (formatted for machine reading). These exclusions may bias the sample toward higher-quality, more carefully curated datasets. The impact on generalizability is not discussed.
evidence: CNN/Daily Mail (Hermann et al., 2015) is anonymized and contains some errors (Chen et al., 2016), so it did not seem to be suitable for annotation.
We considered CBTest (Hill et al., 2016) to be for language modeling tasks rather than RC task and excluded it.
LAMBADA (Paperno et al., 2016)'s texts are formatted for machine reading, and all tokens are lowercased, which seemingly prevents inferences based on proper nouns.
No analysis of how including these datasets would change the main findings.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss the potential bias introduced by excluding these datasets. Conduct a sensitivity analysis: annotate a sample of questions from CNN/Daily Mail or CBTest and report whether the main findings (weak correlation, dataset profiles) hold for these datasets. Acknowledge the limitation that findings may not generalize to all RC datasets.

concerns.title: Confounding factors (genre, curation method, dataset size) not isolated
concerns.description: The six datasets differ in multiple dimensions: genre (narrative vs. expository), curation method (manual vs. automatic), dataset size, task formulation, and answer type. The paper does not isolate the contribution of each factor to the observed dataset profiles. For example, MCTest's 'easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer' profile may be due to genre rather than a fundamental property of the dataset design.
evidence: The corpus' genre (i.e., narrative) seems to reflect the trend of required skills for the questions.
Confounding factors: dataset size, curation method, genre, and task formulation all vary; isolating contribution of each unclear.
No statistical analysis controlling for genre, curation method, or other factors.
Discussion of genre (Section 6) is qualitative, not quantitative.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct a more detailed analysis of confounding factors. For example, compare narrative vs. expository datasets while controlling for other factors. Use regression analysis to estimate the independent contribution of each factor (genre, curation method, etc.) to dataset difficulty. Report effect sizes and confidence intervals.

concerns.title: Applicability of human-oriented readability metrics to RC systems not validated
concerns.description: The paper uses readability metrics designed for human comprehension (Vajjala & Meurers 2012) but acknowledges that 'these metrics were proposed for human readability, they do not necessarily correlate with those for RC systems.' This is a critical assumption (A9) that undermines the main findings. The weak correlations observed may reflect metric mismatch rather than true independence of readability and question difficulty.
evidence: Nonetheless, because these metrics were proposed for human readability, they do not necessarily correlate with those for RC systems. Therefore, in a system analysis, we ideally have to consult various features.
No empirical validation that readability metrics correlate with RC system performance.
No comparison with system-oriented readability measures (e.g., based on neural network activations or error patterns).
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate the applicability of readability metrics to RC systems. Compute correlations between readability metrics and RC system performance (e.g., accuracy, F1 score) on the annotated questions. If correlations are weak, consider alternative readability measures designed for machine comprehension. Discuss the implications for the main findings.

concerns.title: Assumption A1 (skill count = question difficulty) not empirically validated
concerns.description: The paper assumes that the number of required prerequisite skills directly corresponds to question difficulty (A1). This assumption is stated but not validated. No comparison with human difficulty judgments or system performance is provided. If this assumption does not hold, the entire framework for characterizing dataset difficulty becomes invalid.
evidence: From this observation, we assume that the number of required skills corresponds to the difficulty of a question. This is because each skill corresponds to a function of a system, which has to be equipped with the system.
No empirical validation of this assumption.
No correlation between skill count and human difficulty judgments.
No correlation between skill count and RC system performance.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct human studies to validate assumption A1: ask human readers to rate the difficulty of questions and correlate with skill count. Evaluate RC systems on the annotated questions and correlate system accuracy with skill count. Report Spearman rank correlation and p-values. If the correlation is weak, revise the framework or weight skills differently.

concerns.title: MCTest 'difficult-to-answer' claim is questionable given moderate skill count
concerns.description: The paper claims that MCTest is 'easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer,' but Table 3 shows MCTest has an average skill count of 1.56, which is lower than QA4MRE (3.25) and Who-did-What (2.43). If skill count = difficulty (assumption A1), MCTest is not particularly difficult-to-answer. The claim relies on relative comparison and genre-based explanation, not absolute difficulty.
evidence: MCTest is a good example of an RC dataset that is easy to read but difficult to answer.
Table 3: MCTest average 1.56 skills; SQuAD 1.28; MS MARCO 1.19; QA4MRE 3.25; Who-did-What 2.43.
MCTest's skill count is only slightly higher than SQuAD and MS MARCO.
Claim of 'difficult-to-answer' is relative to readability, not absolute.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the claim: MCTest is 'difficult-to-answer relative to its readability' rather than 'difficult-to-answer in absolute terms.' Provide quantitative evidence (e.g., system performance on MCTest vs. other datasets) to support the claim. Consider whether MCTest is better characterized as 'moderate-difficulty-to-answer' rather than 'difficult-to-answer.'

concerns.title: Handling of 'nonsense' and 'no answer' questions is ambiguous and inconsistent
concerns.description: The paper acknowledges ambiguity in identifying 'nonsense' questions and difficulty handling 'no answer' questions. These issues affect the characterization of datasets (e.g., MS MARCO and Who-did-What have higher nonsense rates). The impact on the main findings is not quantified.
evidence: There were questions for which there were disagreements regarding the decision of nonsense. For example, some questions can be solved by external knowledge without seeing their context.
Annotators reported that the prerequisite skills did not easily treat questions whose answer was 'none of the above' in QA4MRE.
Table 2 shows nonsense rates: MS MARCO 14%, Who-did-What 27%, others 1–3%.
No inter-annotator agreement reported specifically for nonsense classification.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide clear operational definitions for 'nonsense' and 'no answer' questions. Report inter-annotator agreement specifically for these categories. Conduct sensitivity analysis: re-analyze the main findings excluding nonsense and 'no answer' questions. Report whether the weak correlation finding holds for the filtered dataset.

comparable_works.relevance: Directly prior work on prerequisite skills for RC; this paper reorganizes and extends the 10-skill taxonomy to 13 skills
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: both use prerequisite skills to characterize RC difficulty. Difference: Sugawara et al. analyzed only 2 datasets (MCTest); this paper analyzes 6 datasets. This paper claims stronger theoretical grounding but provides no empirical comparison.
comparable_works.source_trace: Referenced in Section 1 and Section 3.1; cited as Sugawara et al. (2017)

comparable_works.relevance: Foundational psychological theory for the two-class metric framework; proposes bridging vs. elaboration inferences
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: both use C–I model and bridging/elaboration distinction. Difference: McNamara & Magliano focus on human comprehension; this paper applies the framework to RC dataset evaluation and system development.
comparable_works.source_trace: Referenced throughout Section 2.2 and Section 3; cited as McNamara and Magliano (2009)

comparable_works.relevance: Source of readability metrics used in the paper; proposes 10 linguistic features for readability assessment
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: both use the same 10 readability metrics. Difference: Vajjala & Meurers focus on second-language acquisition; this paper applies metrics to RC dataset evaluation. This paper acknowledges that human-oriented metrics may not correlate with RC system difficulty.
comparable_works.source_trace: Referenced in Section 3.2; cited as Vajjala and Meurers (2012)

comparable_works.relevance: Identifies quality issues in CNN/Daily Mail dataset; justifies sample size of 100 questions per dataset
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: both conduct empirical analysis of RC datasets. Difference: Chen et al. focus on dataset quality and annotation errors; this paper focuses on characterizing datasets along readability and skill dimensions.
comparable_works.source_trace: Referenced in Section 1, Section 2.1, and Section 4.2; cited as Chen et al. (2016)

comparable_works.citation_label: Dagan et al. (2013) and LoBue & Yates (2011)
comparable_works.relevance: Provide classification of entailment phenomena used to ground the 13-skill taxonomy
comparable_works.similarity_or_difference: Similarity: both provide formal frameworks for analyzing linguistic phenomena. Difference: Dagan et al. and LoBue & Yates focus on textual entailment; this paper applies entailment concepts to RC skill classification.
comparable_works.source_trace: Referenced in Section 1 and Section 3.1; cited as Dagan et al. (2013) and LoBue and Yates (2011)

uncertainty_flags: Correlation strength interpretation: 0.025–0.416 range spans weak to moderate; no formal threshold for 'direct correlation' defined; interpretation depends on domain conventions and statistical significance
Sample representativeness: 100 questions per dataset is 10% of typical dataset size; no confidence intervals or bootstrap analysis provided; generalizability to full datasets unclear
Confounding factors: Dataset differences in curation method, genre, task formulation, and size are not isolated; causal mechanisms for observed patterns unclear
Readability metric applicability: Metrics designed for human readability; applicability to RC systems not validated; weak correlations may reflect metric mismatch rather than true independence
Skill taxonomy validation: Theoretical grounding asserted but not empirically tested; no comparison of predictive power vs. prior 10-skill taxonomy; inter-annotator agreement not broken down by skill

Sentence selection reliability: Authors acknowledge inability to evaluate sentence selection competence; impact on skill annotations not quantified; no inter-annotator agreement reported for sentence selection

Generalizability: Findings based on 6 datasets; applicability to future datasets or systems beyond analyzed benchmarks not tested; excluded datasets (CNN/Daily Mail, CBTest, LAMBADA) may have different characteristics
Statistical significance: No significance testing reported for differences between datasets or correlations; unclear if observed patterns are statistically meaningful
Non-linear relationships: Pearson correlation assumes linearity; non-linear or dataset-specific associations not explored; Spearman or Kendall correlations not reported

External knowledge in questions: Authors note ambiguity in identifying questions solvable by external knowledge; impact on 'nonsense' classification unclear; inter-annotator agreement for nonsense classification not reported
Assumption A1 validity: Assumption that skill count = question difficulty is stated but not empirically validated; no correlation with human difficulty judgments or system performance
Assumption A2 validity: Assumption that readability metrics reflect RC system difficulty is acknowledged as potentially invalid; no empirical validation provided
alternative_interpretations: The weak correlations (0.025–0.416) between skill count and readability metrics may not indicate true independence but rather reflect the use of human-oriented readability metrics that do not capture RC system difficulty. If system-oriented readability measures were used, stronger correlations might be observed.

MCTest's characterization as 'easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer' may be an artifact of genre (narrative vs. expository) rather than a fundamental property of dataset design. Narrative texts may inherently require more inference skills (bridging, elaboration) while remaining readable. This does not necessarily support the claim that readability and difficulty are independent.

The 13-skill taxonomy may not be more theoretically grounded than the prior 10-skill taxonomy; the additional skills (Ellipsis, Bridging, Elaboration, Meta-knowledge) may simply be more granular subdivisions of prior categories. Without empirical comparison, the claim of improved theoretical grounding is unsubstantiated.

The weak inter-annotator agreement on sentence selection (not reported) may introduce systematic bias in skill annotations. If annotators systematically over-select or under-select sentences, the observed skill distributions and correlations may not reflect true question difficulty.

The curriculum learning application is speculative and may not work in practice. Systems may not learn better from datasets ordered by this framework if other factors (e.g., dataset size, answer type, context length) are more important for learning.

The paper's finding that readability and difficulty are independent may be specific to the six datasets analyzed and may not generalize to future RC datasets with different characteristics (e.g., longer documents, more complex reasoning, different domains).
transparency_notes: The paper clearly states the research question, methodology, and main findings. The annotation procedure is described in detail, and inter-annotator agreement is reported.

Limitations are acknowledged: inability to evaluate sentence selection competence, ambiguity in identifying nonsense questions, difficulty handling 'no answer' questions, and the fact that readability metrics are human-oriented.
However, the paper does not provide quantitative analysis of how these limitations affect the main findings. Sensitivity analyses are not conducted.

The paper does not report statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or effect sizes for the main findings. This makes it difficult to assess the practical significance of the observed correlations.
The paper does not provide a detailed comparison with the prior 10-skill taxonomy, making it difficult to assess whether the new taxonomy is truly an improvement.

The curriculum learning application is presented as a suggestion without empirical validation. This is appropriately framed as future work, but the speculative nature should be more clearly stated in the abstract and introduction.
The paper makes publicly available the annotation results, which supports reproducibility and future research.
The paper acknowledges that the framework is not dependent on RC models, which supports generalizability. However, applicability to neural systems is not discussed.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper's main contribution—demonstrating weak correlations between readability and question difficulty—is a useful empirical finding but not a novel conceptual insight. The idea that readability and difficulty are independent is intuitive and has been implicitly recognized in prior work (e.g., the examples in Figure 1 are from prior datasets). The 13-skill taxonomy is an incremental refinement of prior work (Sugawara et al. 2017) with stronger theoretical grounding, but this grounding is asserted rather than empirically validated. The two-class metric framework (skills + readability) is a straightforward combination of existing concepts. The curriculum learning application is speculative and not validated. Overall, the paper makes incremental contributions to dataset characterization but lacks significant conceptual novelty.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the paper empirically validated that the 13-skill taxonomy better predicts system performance or human difficulty judgments than the prior 10-skill taxonomy, it would provide stronger evidence for the theoretical grounding claim.

If the paper conducted curriculum learning experiments showing that systems trained on datasets ordered by the proposed framework learn better than systems trained on randomly ordered datasets, it would validate the practical utility of the framework.

If the paper provided system-oriented readability measures (e.g., based on neural network activations or error patterns) and showed stronger correlations with question difficulty, it would address the concern that weak correlations reflect metric mismatch rather than true independence.
If the paper analyzed a larger sample of questions per dataset (e.g., 300–500) and provided confidence intervals, it would strengthen the generalizability of the findings.

If the paper isolated confounding factors (genre, curation method, dataset size) through statistical analysis or controlled experiments, it would provide clearer insights into the drivers of dataset difficulty.
If the paper validated assumption A1 (skill count = question difficulty) through human studies or system performance analysis, it would strengthen the foundation of the entire framework.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper combines existing concepts (prerequisite skills from Sugawara et al. 2017, readability metrics from Vajjala & Meurers 2012, psychological theory from McNamara & Magliano 2009) into a two-class metric framework. The framework itself is not novel; it is a straightforward application of existing ideas to RC dataset evaluation. The 13-skill taxonomy is an incremental refinement of prior work with stronger theoretical grounding, but the grounding is asserted rather than empirically validated.
evidence: The paper explicitly builds on Sugawara et al. (2017)'s 10-skill taxonomy, reorganizing it into 13 skills.
The readability metrics are borrowed from Vajjala & Meurers (2012) without modification.
The psychological theory (C–I model, bridging/elaboration) is from McNamara & Magliano (2009).
The two-class metric framework is a straightforward combination of existing concepts.
uncertainty_flags: The claim that the 13-skill taxonomy is 'more theoretically grounded' is not empirically validated.
The mapping between psychology concepts and NLP entailment phenomena is conceptual, not formal.
The paper does not provide a detailed comparison with the prior 10-skill taxonomy.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper provides empirical evidence that readability and question difficulty are weakly correlated (0.025–0.416) across six RC datasets. This is a useful finding that challenges the implicit assumption that difficult-to-read texts yield difficult questions. However, the finding is not surprising given the examples in Figure 1 (from prior datasets) and the acknowledgment that readability metrics are human-oriented. The dataset characterization (profiles of six datasets) is useful but incremental.
evidence: Table 5 provides correlation coefficients between skill count and readability metrics across six datasets.
Figures 3 and 4 visualize the scatter of datasets in the readability-skill space.
The paper demonstrates that MCTest is easy-to-read but moderate-difficulty-to-answer.
The paper characterizes six datasets along two dimensions, providing comparative insights.
uncertainty_flags: The weak correlations may reflect metric mismatch (human-oriented metrics vs. RC system difficulty) rather than true independence.
No statistical significance testing is reported; unclear if correlations are significantly different from zero.
The finding is based on a small sample (100 questions per dataset); generalizability is unclear.
The paper does not validate that skill count actually corresponds to question difficulty (assumption A1).

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper uses standard annotation procedures (manual labeling with inter-annotator agreement) and standard statistical methods (Pearson correlation). The annotation procedure is transparent and reproducible, but not novel. The paper does not introduce new annotation techniques, statistical methods, or evaluation frameworks.
evidence: The annotation procedure is standard: three annotators label questions with prerequisite skills.
Inter-annotator agreement is computed using standard methods (percentage agreement).
Correlations are computed using Pearson's coefficient, a standard statistical method.
No novel annotation techniques, statistical methods, or evaluation frameworks are introduced.
uncertainty_flags: The paper acknowledges limitations (sentence selection reliability, nonsense classification) but does not propose novel solutions.
The paper does not report Cohen's kappa or other inter-rater reliability measures.
The paper does not use advanced statistical methods (e.g., mixed-effects models, Bayesian analysis) to account for dataset-level variation.

novelty_lenses.lens: Practical impact (utility for practitioners and systems)
novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper provides practical guidance for dataset construction and system development. The two-class metric framework can help practitioners understand dataset characteristics and design datasets with desired properties (e.g., easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer). The curriculum learning application is speculative but potentially useful. However, the practical impact is limited by the lack of empirical validation of the framework's utility.
evidence: The paper provides dataset profiles that characterize six datasets along readability and skill dimensions.
The paper suggests using the framework for curriculum learning, ordering datasets by difficulty for stepwise system development.
The paper provides guidance on dataset construction: attention to genre, question type, and global coherence.
The paper makes annotation results publicly available, supporting future research.
uncertainty_flags: No empirical validation that the framework improves system development or dataset construction.
No experiments showing that curriculum learning with this framework improves system performance.
The practical utility depends on the validity of assumption A1 (skill count = difficulty), which is not empirically validated.
The framework may not generalize to future RC datasets or systems with different architectures.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper makes incremental contributions to RC dataset characterization with solid empirical work (systematic annotation, inter-annotator agreement reporting, comparative analysis across six datasets). However, it has significant methodological limitations: small sample size (100 questions per dataset), lack of statistical significance testing, unvalidated assumptions (A1, A2), and lack of empirical validation of the framework's utility. The main finding (weak correlation between readability and difficulty) is useful but not surprising and may reflect metric mismatch rather than true independence. The 13-skill taxonomy is theoretically motivated but not empirically validated against prior work. The curriculum learning application is speculative. Overall, the paper is methodologically sound but incremental, with limited novelty and unresolved validity concerns. It would be suitable for a workshop or specialized venue but may not meet the bar for a top-tier conference without addressing the methodological limitations and providing empirical validation of key claims.

specialist_reviews.analytical_summary: This paper presents an empirical study that refines and systematizes existing frameworks for evaluating reading comprehension (RC) datasets along two dimensions: prerequisite skills and readability. The core contribution is incremental but methodologically grounded: it reorganizes a prior 10-skill taxonomy into 13 skills with explicit grounding in psychology (Construction-Integration model, bridging/elaboration inferences) and textual entailment theory, then applies this framework alongside readability metrics to characterize six RC datasets. The main empirical finding—that readability and question difficulty are weakly correlated (0.025–0.416)—is presented as evidence that these are independent dimensions worth measuring separately. The paper extends prior work (Sugawara et al. 2017, Sugawara & Aizawa 2016) by broadening the dataset scope (6 vs. 2 datasets), deepening theoretical grounding, and proposing a two-class metric framework for dataset evaluation. However, the novelty is primarily organizational and analytical rather than conceptual: the underlying constructs (prerequisite skills, readability metrics, correlation analysis) are borrowed from prior work, and the paper's main claim—that readability and difficulty are independent—is presented as an empirical observation rather than a novel theoretical insight. The contribution is meaningful for dataset curation and system development but represents an incremental advance in the RC evaluation paradigm.
logical_argument_graph: Premise 1: RC systems require multiple processes (parsing, cohesion, inference) with varying difficulty.
Premise 2: Existing RC datasets are characterized only by superficial categories (question type, answer type), which do not capture difficulty.
Premise 3: McNamara & Magliano (2009) distinguish two aspects of text comprehension: strategic/skilled comprehension and text ease of processing.
Inference 1: These two aspects should be measured separately to characterize RC datasets comprehensively.
Premise 4: Prerequisite skills (from Sugawara et al. 2017) capture strategic/skilled comprehension; readability metrics capture ease of processing.
Inference 2: A refined taxonomy of prerequisite skills, grounded in psychology and entailment theory, provides more theoretically justified classification than prior work.
Premise 5: Annotation of 600 questions (100 per dataset × 6 datasets) with these metrics yields empirical characterization.
Observation 1: Pearson correlations between skill count and readability metrics range from 0.025–0.416 across datasets.
Inference 3: Readability and question difficulty are weakly correlated; they are independent dimensions.
Inference 4: RC datasets can be positioned in a 2D space (readability × difficulty) and ordered by difficulty for curriculum learning.
Conclusion: Two-class metric framework provides more comprehensive dataset evaluation than superficial categories and enables principled dataset construction and system development.

identified_claims.claim_label: Weak correlation between readability and question difficulty
identified_claims.claim_text: Readability of RC dataset texts does not directly correlate with question difficulty; correlations range from 0.025–0.416 across datasets
evidence: Table 5 presents Pearson's correlation coefficients between the number of required prerequisite skills and each readability metric for all questions of the RC datasets. Although there are weak correlations from 0.025 to 0.416, the results highlight that there is not necessarily a strong correlation between the two values.
Figure 3 shows trends of datasets: QA4MRE was relatively difficult both to read and to answer, and SQuAD was difficult to read but easy to answer.
This leads to the following two insights. First, the readability of RC datasets does not directly affect the difficulty of their questions.
uncertainty_flags: Correlation strength interpretation depends on domain conventions; 0.025–0.416 range spans weak to moderate, but no formal threshold for 'direct correlation' is defined
Sample size per dataset is 100 questions; generalizability to larger samples or other datasets not empirically tested
Readability metrics applied only to sentences selected by annotators as necessary; does not reflect full document readability
Pearson correlation assumes linear relationship; non-linear associations not explored
No statistical significance testing reported; p-values and confidence intervals absent
Correlation coefficients may be confounded by dataset-specific factors (genre, curation method, task formulation) not isolated in analysis

identified_claims.claim_label: Easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer datasets are constructible
identified_claims.claim_text: It is possible to construct RC datasets that are easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer, exemplified by MCTest
identified_claims.section_anchor: Section 1, Introduction; Section 5, Results; Section 6, Discussion
evidence: In the second example from MCTest (Richardson et al., 2013), the document is written for children and is easy to read, but the question requires reading multiple sentences and a combination of several skills, such as understanding of causal relations, coreference resolution, and complementing ellipsis.
MCTest is a good example of an RC dataset that is easy to read but difficult to answer. The corpus' genre (i.e., narrative) seems to reflect the trend of required skills for the questions.
Table 4 shows MCTest had the lowest readability scores; Table 3 shows MCTest questions required average 1.56 skills (moderate difficulty).
uncertainty_flags: MCTest is a single exemplar; no systematic construction methodology provided for replicating this property
Difficulty assessment relies on annotator judgment of prerequisite skills; no independent validation against system performance or human difficulty judgments
Genre (narrative vs. expository) is confounded with readability; causal mechanism not isolated
Sample size (100 questions) may not be representative of full MCTest dataset characteristics
Average skill count (1.56) is not substantially higher than SQuAD (1.28) or MS MARCO (1.19); 'difficult-to-answer' is relative and not absolute
No comparison of MCTest question difficulty to other datasets using alternative difficulty metrics

identified_claims.claim_label: Refined 13-skill taxonomy provides theoretically grounded classification
identified_claims.claim_text: A reorganized taxonomy of 13 prerequisite skills (from prior 10-skill work) provides more theoretically grounded classification than previous studies, grounded in psychology (C–I model, bridging/elaboration) and entailment theory
evidence: We reorganized the category of knowledge reasoning in terms of textual entailment and human text comprehension. In research on textual entailment, several methodologies have been proposed for precise analysis of entailment phenomena (Dagan et al., 2013; LoBue and Yates, 2011). In psychology research, Kintsch (1993) proposed dichotomies for the classification of human inferences: retrieved versus generated. In addition, McNamara and Magliano (2009) proposed a similar distinction for inferences: bridging versus elaboration.
Skills 8–10 (Ellipsis, Bridging, Elaboration) are explicitly grounded in psychology and entailment literature.

A problem in previous studies, including that of Sugawara and Aizawa (2016), is that they analyzed only two datasets and that their categorization of knowledge reasoning is provisional with a weak theoretical background.
uncertainty_flags: Theoretical grounding is asserted but not formally validated; no empirical test of whether the 13-skill taxonomy better predicts system performance than prior 10-skill taxonomy
Mapping between psychology concepts (bridging/elaboration) and NLP entailment phenomena is conceptual; no formal alignment procedure described
Inter-annotator agreement (90.1% on 62 questions) is reported globally but not broken down by skill; some skills may have lower reliability
No comparison of annotation consistency between old and new taxonomies; no evidence that new taxonomy is more reliable or predictive
Three new skills (Ellipsis, Bridging, Elaboration, Meta-knowledge) replace one category (commonsense reasoning); it is unclear whether this increases or decreases explanatory power
Skill definitions are descriptive rather than operationalized; boundary conditions between skills (e.g., Bridging vs. Elaboration) may be ambiguous

identified_claims.claim_label: Two-class metric framework characterizes RC datasets more comprehensively
identified_claims.claim_text: Two classes of metrics—prerequisite skills and readability—together characterize RC dataset quality more comprehensively than existing superficial categorizations (e.g., question type, answer type)
evidence: In these situations, it is difficult to assess systems accurately. As Norvig (1989) stated, questions easy for humans often turn out to be difficult for systems.

However, a current problem is that most RC datasets are presented only with superficial categories, such as question types (e.g., what, where, and who) and answer types (e.g., numeric, location, and person).
We adopt two classes of evaluation metrics to show the qualitative features of RC datasets.
uncertainty_flags: Comprehensiveness is asserted but not quantitatively measured; no metric for comparing framework expressiveness
No empirical demonstration that systems trained with knowledge of these two classes perform better than systems trained without
Readability metrics are borrowed from second-language acquisition literature; applicability to RC system development not validated
Framework does not address other potentially relevant dimensions (e.g., answer type, question type, context length, document structure)
No comparison with alternative frameworks for dataset characterization (e.g., linguistic complexity, semantic similarity, information density)
Claim of 'comprehensiveness' is relative; the framework may still miss important dimensions of dataset quality

identified_claims.claim_label: Dataset-specific profiles characterize six RC datasets
identified_claims.claim_text: Different RC datasets exhibit distinct profiles: QA4MRE is difficult on both dimensions; SQuAD is difficult-to-read but easy-to-answer; MCTest is easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer; MS MARCO is easiest; Who-did-What and NewsQA occupy intermediate positions
evidence: QA4MRE seemed to be the most difficult dataset among the RC datasets we analyzed, whereas MS MARCO seemed to be the easiest.
SQuAD was difficult to read along with QA4MRE but relatively easy to answer compared to other datasets.
MCTest is a good example of an RC dataset that is easy to read but difficult to answer.
Table 3: QA4MRE average 3.25 skills; MCTest 1.56; SQuAD 1.28; MS MARCO 1.19.
Table 4: SQuAD and QA4MRE achieved the highest scores in most metrics; MCTest had the lowest scores.
uncertainty_flags: Profiles are based on 100 questions per dataset; may not represent full dataset distributions
Difficulty rankings are relative to this sample; absolute difficulty thresholds not defined
Confounding factors: dataset size, curation method, genre, and task formulation all vary; isolating contribution of each unclear
No statistical significance testing of differences between datasets
Relative rankings may change if different readability metrics or skill definitions are used
Profiles are descriptive rather than predictive; no evidence that these profiles predict system performance or generalization

strengths.title: Systematic annotation study with inter-annotator agreement reporting
strengths.description: The paper annotates 600 questions across 6 RC datasets with prerequisite skills and readability metrics, reporting 90.1% inter-annotator agreement on a sample of 62 questions. This provides a replicable, empirical foundation for dataset characterization.
evidence: Section 4.1: 'We asked three annotators to annotate questions of RC datasets with the prerequisite skills that are required to answer each question.'
Section 5: 'The inter-annotator agreement was 90.1% for 62 randomly sampled questions.'
Appendix A provides detailed sampling methods for each dataset, enabling reproducibility.

strengths.title: Theoretical grounding in psychology and entailment theory
strengths.description: The refined 13-skill taxonomy is explicitly grounded in McNamara & Magliano's (2009) Construction-Integration model, Kintsch's (1993) inference distinctions, and textual entailment literature (Dagan et al., 2013). This provides stronger theoretical justification than the prior 10-skill taxonomy.
evidence: Section 2.2: Detailed exposition of C–I model, bridging/elaboration inferences, and their relevance to RC.
Section 3.1: Skills 8–10 (Ellipsis, Bridging, Elaboration) explicitly map to psychology and entailment concepts.

Introduction: 'A problem in previous studies, including that of Sugawara and Aizawa (2016), is that they analyzed only two datasets and that their categorization of knowledge reasoning is provisional with a weak theoretical background.'

strengths.title: Cross-dataset comparative analysis reveals distinct dataset profiles
strengths.description: The paper characterizes six datasets (QA4MRE, MCTest, SQuAD, Who-did-What, MS MARCO, NewsQA) along two dimensions, revealing that datasets occupy different regions of the readability-difficulty space. This provides actionable insights for dataset selection and curriculum learning.
evidence: Figure 3 and Table 3–4 show distinct profiles: QA4MRE difficult-on-both, SQuAD difficult-to-read/easy-to-answer, MCTest easy-to-read/difficult-to-answer.
Section 5 provides detailed analysis of each dataset's characteristics, including skill frequencies, readability scores, and nonsense rates.
Section 6 discusses practical implications for curriculum learning and system development.

strengths.title: Addresses a recognized gap in RC dataset evaluation
strengths.description: The paper identifies and addresses a genuine limitation in existing RC dataset documentation: most datasets are characterized only by superficial categories (question type, answer type) without deeper analysis of cognitive difficulty or linguistic complexity.
evidence: Introduction: 'However, a current problem is that most RC datasets are presented only with superficial categories, such as question types (e.g., what, where, and who) and answer types (e.g., numeric, location, and person).'
Chen et al. (2016) is cited as evidence that some questions in datasets lack quality to test RC systems.
The paper's two-class framework directly addresses this gap by providing more nuanced characterization.

strengths.title: Acknowledges methodological limitations transparently
strengths.description: The paper explicitly acknowledges several limitations: inability to evaluate sentence selection competence, ambiguity in identifying 'nonsense' questions, treatment of 'no answer' questions, and the fact that readability metrics were designed for humans rather than systems.
evidence: Section 1: 'our methodology could not evaluate the competence of looking for sentences that need to be read and answer candidates from the context.'
Section 6: 'There were questions for which there were disagreements regarding the decision of nonsense. For example, some questions can be solved by external knowledge without seeing their context.'
Section 3.2: 'Nonetheless, because these metrics were proposed for human readability, they do not necessarily correlate with those for RC systems.'

strengths.title: Provides publicly available annotation data
strengths.description: The paper announces that annotation results will be made publicly available, enabling future research and validation of the framework.
evidence: Contributions section: 'We annotate six existing RC datasets with our organized metrics for the comparison and make the results publicly available.'
This supports reproducibility and enables other researchers to build on the work.

concerns.title: Weak correlation finding may reflect metric mismatch rather than true independence
concerns.description: The paper's central empirical finding—that readability and question difficulty are weakly correlated (0.025–0.416)—may be an artifact of using human-oriented readability metrics rather than evidence of true independence. The authors acknowledge this but do not validate the metrics against RC system performance.
evidence: Section 3.2: 'Nonetheless, because these metrics were proposed for human readability, they do not necessarily correlate with those for RC systems. Therefore, in a system analysis, we ideally have to consult various features.'
The weak correlations could indicate that readability metrics designed for human comprehension do not capture the linguistic features that affect RC system performance.
No empirical validation: the paper does not correlate readability metrics with actual RC system performance on these datasets.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Validate readability metrics by correlating them with RC system performance (e.g., accuracy of state-of-the-art systems on each dataset). If system performance correlates more strongly with readability metrics than skill count, the weak correlation finding may be invalidated.

concerns.title: Skill taxonomy refinement is incremental and not empirically validated
concerns.description: The reorganization from 10 to 13 skills is presented as more theoretically grounded, but there is no empirical evidence that the new taxonomy is more predictive of system performance, more reliable across annotators, or more useful for system development than the prior taxonomy.
evidence: Section 3.1: The paper asserts theoretical grounding but provides no comparative analysis with the prior 10-skill taxonomy.
Inter-annotator agreement (90.1%) is reported globally but not broken down by skill, making it unclear whether new skills have lower reliability.
No evidence that the new taxonomy better predicts system performance or human difficulty judgments.
The addition of three new skills (Ellipsis, Bridging, Elaboration) to replace one category (commonsense reasoning) increases granularity but may not increase explanatory power.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Provide a direct comparison: (1) re-annotate a subset of questions using the old 10-skill taxonomy and compare inter-annotator agreement; (2) correlate both taxonomies with RC system performance on the annotated datasets; (3) demonstrate that the new taxonomy better predicts system performance or human difficulty judgments.

concerns.title: Sample size (100 questions per dataset) may not represent full dataset distributions
concerns.description: The paper annotates only 100 questions per dataset, which is approximately 10% of typical dataset sizes. Confidence intervals, bootstrap resampling, or sensitivity analysis would strengthen claims about dataset-level properties.
evidence: Section 4.2: 'For the annotation, we randomly selected 100 questions from each dataset in Table 1. This amount of questions was considered to be sufficient for the analysis of RC datasets as performed by Chen et al. (2016).'
The justification relies on a single prior study (Chen et al. 2016) without independent validation.
Figures 3–4 show scatter plots of individual questions, revealing substantial variation within datasets; a sample of 100 may not capture this variation.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute 95% confidence intervals for skill counts and readability metrics using bootstrap resampling. Test whether increasing sample size (e.g., to 200 or 300 questions) changes the conclusions about dataset profiles or correlations.

concerns.title: No statistical significance testing reported for correlations or dataset differences
concerns.description: Table 5 presents Pearson correlation coefficients without p-values or confidence intervals. Differences between datasets (e.g., average skill counts in Table 3) are not tested for statistical significance.
evidence: Table 5: Correlation coefficients are reported without p-values, confidence intervals, or significance levels.
Table 3: Average skill counts range from 1.19 (MS MARCO) to 3.25 (QA4MRE), but no statistical test of differences is provided.
The paper does not report whether correlations are significantly different from zero or significantly different across datasets.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report p-values and 95% confidence intervals for all correlation coefficients in Table 5. Conduct ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis tests to determine whether average skill counts differ significantly across datasets. Report effect sizes (e.g., Cohen's d) for pairwise comparisons.

concerns.title: Readability metrics applied only to selected sentences, not full documents
concerns.description: Readability metrics are computed only on sentences annotators identified as necessary to answer questions, not on full documents. This may bias metric distributions and correlations, and does not reflect the readability difficulty experienced by systems that must process entire documents.
evidence: Section 3.2: 'We applied these metrics only to sentences that needed to be read to answer questions.'

Section 6: 'As a brief analysis, we further investigated sentences in the context of the datasets that were highlighted in the annotation. Analyses were performed in two ways: for each question, we counted the number of required sentences and their distance.'

Table 6 shows that average number of required sentences ranges from 1.04 (SQuAD) to 1.18 (MCTest), suggesting that most questions require only 1–2 sentences. This may artificially reduce readability metric variance.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute readability metrics on both selected sentences and full documents. Compare metric distributions and correlations. Discuss how the restriction to selected sentences affects the interpretation of readability scores and correlations.

concerns.title: Pearson correlation assumes linearity; non-linear relationships not explored
concerns.description: The paper uses Pearson correlation to measure association between skill count and readability metrics. If the relationship is non-linear, monotonic but non-linear, or mediated by dataset-specific factors, Pearson correlation will underestimate or mischaracterize the association.
evidence: Table 5: Only Pearson correlation coefficients are reported; Spearman rank correlation or other measures are not provided.
Figures 3–4 show scatter plots that suggest possible non-linear or dataset-specific patterns (e.g., QA4MRE, MCTest, and SQuAD occupy distinct clusters).
The paper does not explore whether the relationship between skills and readability varies by dataset, genre, or other factors.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report Spearman rank correlation coefficients in addition to Pearson correlations. Fit non-linear models (e.g., polynomial regression, LOESS) and compare goodness-of-fit. Conduct separate correlation analyses for each dataset to test for dataset-specific effects.

concerns.title: Sentence selection reliability not quantified; impact on skill annotations unclear
concerns.description: The paper acknowledges that it cannot evaluate annotators' competence in selecting necessary sentences, but does not quantify inter-annotator agreement specifically for sentence selection or conduct sensitivity analysis to show how variation in sentence selection affects skill annotations.
evidence: Section 1: 'our methodology could not evaluate the competence of looking for sentences that need to be read and answer candidates from the context.'
Section 6: 'As mentioned in Section 1, our methodology cannot evaluate the competence of selecting sentences that need to be read to answer questions.'
No inter-annotator agreement is reported for sentence selection; only global agreement (90.1%) is reported.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report inter-annotator agreement specifically for sentence selection (e.g., Jaccard similarity of selected sentence sets). Conduct sensitivity analysis: re-annotate a subset of questions with different sentence selections and measure how this affects skill annotations and correlations.

concerns.title: Framework does not address other potentially relevant dimensions of dataset quality
concerns.description: The paper claims that the two-class framework (skills + readability) provides 'comprehensive' characterization, but does not address other dimensions that may affect RC system performance: answer type, question type, context length, document structure, semantic similarity between question and context, etc.
evidence: Introduction: 'However, a current problem is that most RC datasets are presented only with superficial categories, such as question types (e.g., what, where, and who) and answer types (e.g., numeric, location, and person).'
The paper dismisses question type and answer type as 'superficial' but does not provide evidence that these dimensions are less important than skills and readability.
No comparison with alternative frameworks for dataset characterization.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Acknowledge that the framework is not exhaustive. Discuss other potentially relevant dimensions (answer type, question type, context length, semantic similarity) and explain why they were excluded or deprioritized. Provide evidence that skills and readability are more predictive of system performance than these alternative dimensions.

concerns.title: Ambiguity in identifying 'nonsense' questions affects dataset characterization
concerns.description: The paper acknowledges that annotators disagreed on whether questions are 'nonsense' or solvable by external knowledge, but does not quantify this disagreement or conduct sensitivity analysis to show how different filtering criteria affect dataset profiles.
evidence: Section 6: 'There were questions for which there were disagreements regarding the decision of nonsense. For example, some questions can be solved by external knowledge without seeing their context.'
Appendix A: Different filtering criteria are applied to different datasets (e.g., NewsQA is filtered by 'is_question_bad = 0'; MS MARCO by 'is_selected = 1').

Table 2 shows that nonsense rates vary substantially across datasets (1% for MCTest and NewsQA; 27% for Who-did-What), but it is unclear whether these differences reflect true dataset properties or annotation ambiguity.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report inter-annotator agreement specifically for the 'nonsense' judgment. Conduct sensitivity analysis: re-analyze dataset profiles using different filtering criteria (e.g., include all questions, exclude all ambiguous cases, use majority vote) and show how conclusions change.

concerns.title: Curriculum learning application is speculative and not empirically validated
concerns.description: Section 6 proposes using the framework for curriculum learning (training systems on datasets ordered by difficulty), but provides no empirical evidence that this approach improves system performance or learning curves.
evidence: Section 6: 'One example for the development of an RC system is that it should be built to solve an easy-to-read and easy-to-answer dataset. The next step is to improve the system so that it can solve an easy-to-read and difficult-to-answer dataset. Finally, only after it can solve such dataset should the system be applied to a difficult-to-read and difficult-to-answer dataset.'
This is presented as a suggestion, not as an empirically validated finding.
No comparison with alternative training strategies or evidence that curriculum learning based on this framework outperforms random or other orderings.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Either remove the curriculum learning discussion as speculative, or provide empirical validation: train RC systems on datasets ordered by difficulty (as defined by the framework) and measure learning curves. Compare with random ordering and other curriculum learning strategies.

concerns.title: Dataset exclusion rationale may introduce bias
concerns.description: The paper excludes CNN/Daily Mail, CBTest, and LAMBADA from annotation due to quality concerns or task formulation differences. However, these exclusions may bias the sample toward higher-quality datasets and affect the generalizability of findings.
evidence: Section 4.2: 'CNN/Daily Mail (Hermann et al., 2015) is anonymized and contains some errors (Chen et al., 2016), so it did not seem to be suitable for annotation. We considered CBTest (Hill et al., 2016) to be for language modeling tasks rather than RC task and excluded it. LAMBADA (Paperno et al., 2016)'s texts are formatted for machine reading, and all tokens are lowercased, which seemingly prevents inferences based on proper nouns.'

These exclusions are justified but may introduce bias if the excluded datasets have different characteristics (e.g., higher nonsense rates, different skill distributions) that would affect conclusions.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Discuss potential bias introduced by dataset exclusions. If possible, annotate a sample of questions from excluded datasets and compare their profiles to included datasets. Alternatively, conduct sensitivity analysis: assume different profiles for excluded datasets and show how this affects conclusions.

concerns.title: Novelty is primarily organizational rather than conceptual
concerns.description: The paper's main contribution is organizing and systematizing existing constructs (prerequisite skills, readability metrics, correlation analysis) rather than introducing novel concepts or methods. The core finding—that readability and difficulty are independent—is presented as an empirical observation rather than a theoretical insight.
evidence: The 13-skill taxonomy is a refinement of Sugawara et al.'s (2017) 10-skill taxonomy, not a novel framework.
Readability metrics are borrowed from Vajjala & Meurers (2012); no new metrics are proposed.
Correlation analysis is standard statistical methodology; no novel analytical methods are introduced.
The main empirical finding (weak correlation between readability and difficulty) is presented as a descriptive observation, not as a theoretical contribution.
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the paper's positioning as an incremental contribution that refines and systematizes existing work. Emphasize the practical value of the framework for dataset curation and system development rather than claiming conceptual novelty.

uncertainty_flags: Correlation strength interpretation: 0.025–0.416 range spans weak to moderate; no formal threshold for 'direct correlation' defined; interpretation depends on domain conventions and context
Sample representativeness: 100 questions per dataset is ~10% of typical dataset size; confidence intervals or bootstrap analysis would strengthen claims about dataset-level properties
Confounding factors: Dataset differences in curation method, genre, task formulation, and size are not isolated; causal mechanisms unclear
Readability metric applicability: Metrics designed for human readability; applicability to RC systems not validated; weak correlations may reflect metric mismatch rather than true independence
Skill taxonomy validation: Theoretical grounding asserted but not empirically tested; no comparison of predictive power vs. prior 10-skill taxonomy; inter-annotator agreement not broken down by skill
Sentence selection reliability: Authors acknowledge inability to evaluate sentence selection competence; impact on skill annotations not quantified
Generalizability: Findings based on 6 datasets; applicability to future datasets or systems beyond analyzed benchmarks not tested
Statistical significance: No significance testing reported for differences between datasets or correlations; p-values and confidence intervals absent
Non-linear relationships: Pearson correlation assumes linearity; non-linear or dataset-specific associations not explored
External knowledge in questions: Authors note ambiguity in identifying questions solvable by external knowledge; impact on 'nonsense' classification unclear
Genre confounding: MCTest's narrative genre is confounded with readability; causal mechanism not isolated from other dataset properties
alternative_interpretations: The weak correlation between readability and difficulty (0.025–0.416) may reflect a mismatch between human-oriented readability metrics and RC system difficulty, rather than true independence of these dimensions. If metrics were designed for systems rather than humans, correlations might be stronger.

The 13-skill taxonomy may not be more predictive or reliable than the prior 10-skill taxonomy; the reorganization may simply increase granularity without improving explanatory power. Empirical comparison is needed.

MCTest's characterization as 'easy-to-read but difficult-to-answer' may be an artifact of genre (narrative vs. expository) rather than a fundamental property of the dataset. Other narrative datasets might show similar patterns.
The framework's 'comprehensiveness' is relative; other dimensions (answer type, question type, context length, semantic similarity) may be equally or more important for predicting system performance.
The weak correlations may be confounded by dataset-specific factors (curation method, size, task formulation) that are not isolated in the analysis. Dataset-specific correlations might be stronger.

The curriculum learning suggestion is speculative and may not improve system performance; alternative training strategies (e.g., random ordering, difficulty-agnostic sampling) might be equally or more effective.
The sample of 100 questions per dataset may not be representative; full-dataset analysis might reveal different patterns or stronger correlations.
Inter-annotator agreement of 90.1% on 62 questions may not generalize to the full 600-question set; some skills or datasets may have lower agreement.
transparency_notes: This review assesses the paper as an incremental contribution that refines and systematizes existing frameworks (prerequisite skills, readability metrics) rather than introducing novel concepts. The contribution is meaningful for dataset curation and system development but represents an organizational advance rather than a conceptual breakthrough.

The paper's central empirical finding—that readability and question difficulty are weakly correlated—is presented as evidence of independence, but may reflect a mismatch between human-oriented readability metrics and RC system difficulty. The authors acknowledge this limitation but do not validate metrics against system performance.

The refined 13-skill taxonomy is theoretically grounded in psychology and entailment theory, but lacks empirical validation. No evidence is provided that the new taxonomy is more predictive, reliable, or useful than the prior 10-skill taxonomy.

The paper acknowledges several methodological limitations (sentence selection reliability, ambiguity in 'nonsense' classification, applicability of human readability metrics to systems) but does not quantify their impact or conduct sensitivity analysis.

Statistical rigor is limited: no significance testing is reported for correlations or dataset differences; confidence intervals and p-values are absent; sample size (100 questions per dataset) is justified by a single prior study without independent validation.
The curriculum learning application (Section 6) is speculative and not empirically validated; no evidence is provided that ordering datasets by difficulty improves system performance.
The paper's scope is limited to 6 datasets; generalizability to future datasets or systems beyond the analyzed benchmarks is not tested.

This review separates novelty risk (organizational/incremental contribution) from methodological flaws (statistical rigor, sample size, validation). The paper has moderate methodological concerns but lower conceptual novelty risk.

creativity_safeguard.novelty_not_validity_note: The paper's contribution is primarily organizational and incremental: it refines the prior 10-skill taxonomy, applies it to 6 datasets (vs. 2 in prior work), and introduces readability metrics as a second dimension. The core finding—that readability and difficulty are weakly correlated—is presented as an empirical observation rather than a novel theoretical insight. Close analogs exist in prior work (Sugawara et al. 2017, McNamara & Magliano 2009, Vajjala & Meurers 2012), and the paper builds directly on these foundations. The contribution is meaningful but not disruptive.
counterfactual_conditions_for_success: If the paper provided empirical validation that the 13-skill taxonomy better predicts system performance than the prior 10-skill taxonomy, the contribution would be stronger.
If the paper validated readability metrics against RC system performance and showed that weak correlations reflect true independence (not metric mismatch), the main finding would be more convincing.
If the paper conducted curriculum learning experiments and demonstrated that ordering datasets by difficulty improves system performance, the practical value would be demonstrated.
If the paper reported statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, and sensitivity analysis, methodological rigor would be substantially improved.
If the paper compared the two-class framework with alternative frameworks for dataset characterization and showed superior predictive power, the claim of 'comprehensiveness' would be justified.
If the paper analyzed the full datasets (not just 100 questions per dataset) and conducted cross-dataset generalization tests, generalizability claims would be stronger.

novelty_lenses.rationale: The paper refines and systematizes existing frameworks (prerequisite skills, readability metrics) and applies them to a broader set of datasets (6 vs. 2 in prior work). The theoretical grounding is strengthened by explicit connection to psychology and entailment theory. However, the core concepts and methods are borrowed from prior work; the main contribution is organizational rather than conceptual. The empirical finding (weak correlation between readability and difficulty) is presented as an observation rather than a novel insight.
evidence: The 13-skill taxonomy is a refinement of Sugawara et al.'s (2017) 10-skill taxonomy, not a novel framework.
Readability metrics are borrowed from Vajjala & Meurers (2012); no new metrics are proposed.
The two-class framework is grounded in McNamara & Magliano (2009); the paper applies existing theory to RC datasets.
The main empirical finding (weak correlation) is presented as a descriptive observation, not as a theoretical contribution.
